turns.speaker: host
turns.text: One of the big questions on people's minds these days, is AI doing bad things? As someone that watches these models think and operate, why is it so hard to catch it thinking badly trying to deceive us?
turns.zh: 如今很多人心里最大的一个问题就是：AI 会不会干坏事？作为一个天天盯着这些模型怎么思考、怎么运转的人，为什么这么难发现它心里在想坏主意、想骗我们？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We trained Claude to be helpful, harmless, and honest. Is it the case that it's behaving well, but if you look inside actually it's like, oh, I'm only behaving well because Lenny's watching right now.
turns.zh: 我们把 Claude 训练成有帮助、无害、诚实的。可要是往里看，它会不会其实是这样：哦，我只是因为 Lenny 在看着才表现良好。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: People's full-time jobs is studying the model, how it thinks, how it operates. How long has this been a skillset and a job?
turns.zh: 有个人的全职工作就是研究这个模型，看它怎么想、怎么运转。这门手艺、这份职业，存在多久了？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: One of the most important things to realize if you use language models or think about them is just this very bizarre fact that to make them is not to understand them. All these models do is just a lot of mathematical operations on many numbers. If you look at it, it makes no sense. You just have a list of a hundred numbers, the model's doing math, and then you just try to see if there's patterns.
turns.zh: 如果你在用语言模型，或者在思考语言模型，最该先记住的一件怪事就是：造出它们并不等于理解它们。这些模型所做的，就是对一大堆数字做大量数学运算。你去看它，根本看不出意义——你只拿到一百个数字，模型在做数学运算，然后你只能试着从中找规律。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: You are figuring it out the same way we figure out how the brain works, looking for patterns. You show this image, this part of the brain lights up and you're doing the exact same thing with AI. Wow, this is so fascinating.
turns.zh: 你们摸索的方式，和我们研究大脑的方式一模一样：找规律。给这张图看，大脑这块亮起来；你们对 AI 做的就是同样的事。哇，这太有意思了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There was this model we were training, it would go crazy. It would do some math, it would get to an answer, I think it was 12. It would immediately go back and say like, "Oh no, oh my God, the answer actually is for sure 36." It would do math again, it would get to 12. Slowly it would start descending into madness, writing in all caps, literally saying, "I'm possessed by a demon."
turns.zh: 我们训练时有过一个模型，它会突然发疯。它算一道数学题，得出一个答案，我记得是 12，它马上回过头说：哦不，天哪，答案肯定是 36。它再算一遍，又得到 12。它慢慢滑向疯狂，开始全大写地写字，字面意义上说：「我被恶魔附身了。」

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Humans, if you really boil it down, we're basically next token predictors ourselves. We're just trying to figure out the next thing to say. Dario is always out there, "This is really dangerous. We got to be really careful." And everyone's just like, "No, he's just saying that for marketing reasons." And now it's like, wait, shit, it's really dangerous.
turns.zh: 人类如果真往深了想，本质上也是下一个词预测器——我们不过是在琢磨下一句该说什么。Dario 总在那儿说「这真的很危险，我们得非常非常小心」，所有人都是：得了吧，他不过是为了营销才那么说。现在大家的反应变成了：等等，靠，这真的很危险。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Take the idea that this technology is going to keep improving seriously.
turns.zh: 先假设这项技术会持续显著变强。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Do you think about consciousness as a part of this? Just do you think AI is conscious?
turns.zh: 你会把意识也纳入考虑吗？你觉得 AI 有意识吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, man.
turns.zh: 哎呀。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Emmanuel, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Emmanuel，非常感谢你来，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，Lenny。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So you work on interpretability at Anthropic. Explain what that is. Explain what it is you do.
turns.zh: 你在 Anthropic 做可解释性。解释一下这是什么意思，也解释一下你具体在做什么。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. So I work in a team of interpretability researchers and our goal is to understand how LLMs like Claude work by looking inside them.
turns.zh: 好。我所在的团队是一群可解释性研究员，我们的目标是通过「往里看」来理解 Claude 这样的 LLM 是怎么运作的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: One of the most important things to realize if you use language models or think about them is just this very bizarre fact that to make them is not to understand them. You make them by building this architecture, which is kind of like a scaffold, and then you pass a bunch of data through them and they grow in inscrutable ways.
turns.zh: 如果你在用语言模型，或者在思考语言模型，最该先记住的一件怪事就是：造出它们并不等于理解它们。你造它的方式是先搭出这么一套架构，有点像一副脚手架，然后把大量数据灌进去，它们就以难以参透的方式生长出来。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so that's why it's even a thing that we could be wanting to do to study how these models work.
turns.zh: 所以，研究这些模型到底怎么运作，本身才成了一件值得做的事。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so a lot of our research has been on, well, when the models are about to produce one more word, there's actually a whole universe of stuff that happens and we try to untangle as much of it as we can.
turns.zh: 我们的研究有很大一部分聚焦于：当模型正要吐出下一个词的时候，其实有一整个宇宙的事情正在发生，我们尽力去把这团乱麻理清楚。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: There's going to be a lot of mind-expanding, I don't know, elements to this conversation I expect. One is along these lines, this point that you make that models are not built, they're grown. Speak more to that.
turns.zh: 这场对话我估计会有很多让人脑子被撑开的元素。其中一个就是你刚才说的这一点：模型不是被「造」出来的，是被「长」出来的。再展开说说？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: At a really high level, the way a model like Claude works is you train it in these successive phases, like the first phase, which people refer to as pre-training is you just take a large corpus of data, and over this corpus of data, you feed the model as input, the let's say first half of a certain document, and you ask it to predict the word that comes next.
turns.zh: 从很高的层面看，Claude 这样的模型是这样训练的：分几个阶段依次来。第一阶段大家叫预训练，你只是拿一大堆语料，在这堆语料上，把某份文档的前半段喂给模型，然后让它预测接下来那个词。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Then you do that again and again and again and again for an ungodly amount of data. And after you do that, there's then this other phase where then you have this fine-tuning phase where maybe instead of arbitrary data, you have a corpus of examples of how the model should behave and that's what you train it on.
turns.zh: 然后你对海量数据一遍又一遍地重复这件事，量大到离谱。做完之后还有另一个阶段，叫微调：这一阶段喂的不再是随便的数据，而是一批示范模型该怎样表现的例子，你就在这些例子上训练。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So you have examples of dialogue of helpful assistant telling you your favorite recipe or solving coding problems. And then there's further details here that I'm just going to skip for a second. But then, okay, so what does that mean that you're doing this process? What is this thing that you're training?
turns.zh: 比如有帮助的助手告诉你拿手菜谱的对话，或者帮你解决编程问题的对话。还有些细节我先跳过。那么问题来了：你做这一整套流程，究竟是在训练什么东西？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: All models are, is they take this input, which is a bunch of words, they turn these words into numbers, and then they do some math on these numbers and they get some intermediate results and then they do more math and they get some intermediate results and they do this again and again and again and again many times. And then at the end they have a final result which then convert back into a word.
turns.zh: 所有模型都是这样：把输入（一堆词）变成数字，在这些数字上做一些运算，得到一些中间结果，再做更多运算，又得到一些中间结果，如此一遍又一遍地反复很多次。最后得到一个结果，再把它变回一个词。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so the math that they do, these computations, that's the part that's grown. That's the part where it's just like through learning to do this task better, we serve update parameters in one direction or another and then they learn some formulas. We have no idea what they are.
turns.zh: 所以它做的这些数学运算、这些计算，才是那个「长出来」的部分。模型通过学习把任务做得更好，我们就朝某个方向更新参数，然后它们学会了一些公式。我们完全不知道这些公式是什么。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And the goal of my team is to study both what these formulas mean in the end and also what these intermediate results are. Can we decode them and can we see what the model is doing as it's doing all of this intermediate stuff?
turns.zh: 我团队的目标，就是既研究这些公式最后到底意味着什么，也研究这些中间结果是什么。我们能把它们解码出来吗？能在模型做这一大堆中间运算的过程中，看清它在干什么吗？

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does it blow your mind as much as it blows mind that we have some code that we wrote that first of all, we have to now kind of watch and study like a neuroscientist studies a brain, that's a new thing that we need to be doing to understand what the hell is going on?
turns.zh: 我们写出来的一些代码，如今必须像神经科学家研究大脑那样去盯着、去研究，这件事本身会不会一样让你觉得震撼？这是件全新事，我们得靠它才能搞清楚到底发生了什么。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And then this idea that this terminology using is how a lot of people think about this. It's like we've created this new life, artificial life, artificial intelligence. It's pretty mind-boggling if you really think about it and kind of zoom out.
turns.zh: 还有那套说法：很多人是这么理解这件事的——我们创造了某种新的生命，人工生命、人工智能。你真拉远一点看，这事挺让人头皮发麻的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think it's really weird. I think that the best way to think about it is the reason we ended up here, one of the big reasons is that we don't know how to do it the normal programming way.
turns.zh: 我觉得这确实很奇怪。我觉得最好的理解方式是：我们之所以走到这一步，一个重要原因是我们不知道用常规编程的办法怎么做成这件事。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So you want to build an app or something, you want to do something pretty self-contained, you can just have a programmer that's going to write a bunch of rules and say, "Ah, well, if somebody clicks on this button, then this happens." If this, then that, and so on.
turns.zh: 你想做个 app，或者做点相当自成一体的东西，那没问题，找个程序员写一堆规则就行：「如果有人点了这个按钮，就发生这个；如果这样，就那样」，诸如此类。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We don't know how to write that software for classifying images into categories or for making a machine that can generally take in arbitrary text and produce texts. It can take in reports and summarize them, can write emails.
turns.zh: 但把图片分到各个类别，或者造一台能普遍接收任意文本又产出文本的机器——我们不知道怎么写这种软件。它能读报告并做总结，能写邮件。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so in a sense, it's weird that this very simple kind of training objective gets you all the way there. But in another sense, it's also, I almost feel like there's a sense of it's impressive and it means something.
turns.zh: 所以从某种意义上说，如此简单的训练目标居然能把你一路带到那里，这本身很奇怪。但换个角度，它又让人印象深刻，而且是有意义的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It means that what you think is a simple objective, this like, oh, we're just feeding data and predict the next thing is probably deceptively complicated. We're probably doing more than what it sounds like. And I think a lot of the ways that maybe I've updated on how these models work is by realizing how complicated it is to do what they do well.
turns.zh: 它意味着：你以为很简单的东西——哦，我们就是喂数据、预测下一个词——其实复杂得超出表面。我们做的恐怕比字面上听起来要多得多。我对模型工作方式的很多认识更新，来自意识到要把它们做的事做好到底有多难。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Say more about that. What do you think about when you say it's this kind of unexpected complication?
turns.zh: 展开说说。你说这是种出人意料的复杂性，你指的是什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Okay. So one way to think about next token prediction that I think a lot of people think about is your iPhone auto-complete where you write some text and then it'll predict the next word and it's maybe right, I don't know, 60% of the time and then kind of funny and weird the rest of the time.
turns.zh: 好。人们对「下一个词预测」的一个理解方式，我觉得很多人都这么想：iPhone 的自动补全——你写点文字，它预测下一个词，可能对吧，我也不知道，六成概率对，剩下的时候就会蹦出些滑稽又古怪的东西。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And I would think of that as sort of the easiest version of predicting the next word. And unfortunately, I think that's the mental model that people have for these models.
turns.zh: 我会把这看作预测下一个词最简单的那个版本。遗憾的是，我觉得人们对这些模型的心智模型就是这一套。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: But if you get better at that and language models got better at predicting the next word than humans in around 2019, if you keep getting better at that, you start running out of easy words. So initially you just had to predict simple sentence structure. Later on, the model has to predict simple facts about the world.
turns.zh: 但如果你把这事做得越来越好——语言模型大概在 2019 年前后就比人类更会预测下一个词——你会发现简单词已经不够用了。刚开始你只需要预测简单的句子结构；再往后，模型得预测关于世界的基本事实。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: If I complete a sentence like, "Oh, the capital of France is," and has to be like, "Okay, that's Paris." And once it's good at that and it keeps improving, the only thing that's left is predicting the answer of some complex physics equation or the final paragraph of some PhD thesis.
turns.zh: 比如你补全一句「哦，法国的首都是——」，答案得是「巴黎」。等它连这个也做得好、而且还在继续变强，那剩下的就只有预测某个复杂物理方程的答案，或者某篇博士论文的最后一段了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so I think that you end up realizing if you think about this is that, man, predicting the hardest words is actually extremely hard to do and it's a sort of mystery how you would be able to do that. And to me, this has been a motivation of why I even started studying these models in the first place.
turns.zh: 所以你会意识到：天哪，预测最难的那些词其实是极难的事，而你能做到这一点本身简直是个谜。这对我来说，正是我当初为什么会开始研究这些模型。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I was like, "How can something so simple give rise to something so powerful?" And it's like, well, if you think about the model that has to predict the... One example I always like to use is the capital of the state that contains Dallas is, and it'll say Austin.
turns.zh: 我当时想的是：「怎么可能这么简单的东西，长出这么强大的东西？」比如我喜欢用的一个例子是：「包含达拉斯的那个州的首都是——」，它会说奥斯汀。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Well, to do that well, at least for you and me, you have to have a mental model of the geography at play. You have to be like, "Oh, where's Dallas? Dallas is in Texas. States have capitals. The capital of Texas is Austin," and so on. And so as these models get better at the seemingly simple task, the best way to solve it, at least for us, is to just understand the underlying structure of the world.
turns.zh: 要把这事做对，至少对你我来说，你得在脑子里有一幅地理模型：达拉斯在哪儿？在得州；州有首府；得州的首府是奥斯汀，诸如此类。所以当这些模型把这个看似简单的任务做得越来越好时，对我们来说最好的解法，其实就是理解世界底层的结构。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And in fact, some of the stuff that we look at inside model shows that they do understand that and they do sort of manipulate these concepts like we do.
turns.zh: 事实上，我们往模型内部看到的一些东西表明，它们确实理解这一点，也确实像我们一样摆弄这些概念。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Oh man, there's so much there. One is just this kind of idea, I forget who said this, maybe Ilya, this idea that to predict the next token wall, you basically have to understand the entire universe.
turns.zh: 天哪，这里面的东西太多了。其中一个，我忘了是谁说的，可能是 Ilya：要想预测下一个词，你基本上得理解整个宇宙。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: He has an example that I love too where he has the example like predict and the murderer was at the end of a mystery novel. It's like, well, to do that, you kind of have to have understood the whole plot.
turns.zh: 他有个我也很喜欢的例子：比如要预测「凶手是那部悬疑小说结尾的人」。你得先理解整个剧情才做得到。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah. The other, I forget who tweeted this idea that humans, if you really boil it down, we're basically next token predictors ourselves. We're just trying to figure out the next thing to say. And if you meditate, you start to actually notice your brain wanting to do things and say things. I don't know how much meditation you've done, but it feels like you start to pay attention to your own next token predictor.
turns.zh: 对。还有一个，我忘了是谁发推说的：人类如果真往深了剥，本质上也是下一个词预测器，我们只是在琢磨下一句该说什么。而且如果你冥想，就会真的注意到自己大脑里那股想做事、想说话的冲动。我不知道你冥想过多少，但感觉就像你开始留意起自己这个「下一个词预测器」了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, yeah. Yeah. A thing I think about often is that right now as I'm answering you, there's two things going on in my mind. There's hopefully more than two, but at least two. And one of them is there's sort of a point I'm leading you to. There's a broad idea I'm trying to land the sentence on.
turns.zh: 哦，对。我经常想的一件事是：此刻我在回答你的过程中，我脑子里至少同时有两件事在发生。希望不止两件，但至少两件。其一是有一个我正要把你引向的点，有一个我正努力让这句话落上去的宽泛想法。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And the other thing is, at the same time, I'm just predicting the next thing to say. I'm just saying one word at a time and I'm making sentences and I'm trying to make them make sense and I'm pausing when I think it makes sense. But at the end of the day, even though I'm just saying one word at a time, all along, what I wanted to do is to compare this process to what language models do.
turns.zh: 另一件是，同一时间里我就是在预测下一句要说什么。我只是一次说一个词，把它们拼成句子，试着让它们说得通，觉得说得通了就停顿一下。但说到底，即便我一次只说一个词，这一路我真正想做的，还是把这个过程跟语言模型做的事情做比较。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I'm curious what else as you spend time paying attention to how LLMs work and operate. I feel like you're in the top 0.1 percentile of people that have studied and watched LLMs operate and think. What else has surprised you about how they operate and think?
turns.zh: 你花了这么多时间去观察 LLM 的运作，我很好奇还有别的什么让你吃惊的。我觉得你是研究、观察 LLM 怎么思考和运转的人里属于前 0.1% 的那批。它们怎么运作、怎么思考，还有什么别的让你意外？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's so much. So maybe I'll go through rather than... There's a bunch of findings, but then maybe there's how they've changed how I think about models.
turns.zh: 太多太多了。我可能不按「发现清单」来讲，而是讲这些发现怎么改变了我对模型的理解。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So to go back to the capital example, this sort of ask the model, "The capital of the state that contains Dallas is?" So one question that people have had for a while is how do these models answer questions like this?
turns.zh: 回到刚才首都那个例子：问模型「包含达拉斯的那个州的首都是——」。有个问题人们问了很久：这些模型是怎么回答这种问题的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Is it that they've seen just so much text that they've kind of memorized lists of prompts and responses, or is it that they're having some sort of model of what you're actually asking about that you're actually asking back cities and cities are in states and states are in countries and things like that.
turns.zh: 是因为它读了太多文本、把一批问答的清单背下来了；还是因为它对你真正在问的东西有某种模型——你在问城市，城市属于州，州属于国家之类的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so one thing that we do on my team is we ask a question like this and then we look inside the model at these intermediate results.
turns.zh: 我们团队的做法之一，就是问这样一个问题，然后往模型内部去看那些中间结果。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Before it produces a given word, as it's about to answer, we just look at the intermediate results and we basically have an immense amount of effort dedicated to trying to decode what these intermediate results mean.
turns.zh: 在它吐出某个词之前、正要回答的时候，我们就去看这些中间结果。我们投入了极大的精力，去解码这些中间结果到底意味着什么。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And if we decode them well, which we can do in some cases, we can see that models often have and represent these concepts.
turns.zh: 如果我们解得好——在某些情况下确实能做到——就能看到模型往往拥有并表示着这些概念。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So when you ask that Dallas question, what you see is inside the model, you see the representation, you see an intermediate result that maps the representation of Texas that lights up and one to capitals, and then those two combine to activate an intermediate result.
turns.zh: 所以当你问那个达拉斯的问题时，你会在模型内部看到：你看到一个表示「得州」被点亮的表示，以及一个表示「首府」的表示，然后这两者结合，激活出另一个中间结果。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's like, "Oh, the capital of Texas, that's Austin." They have representations like this for basically everything, every concept that you can think of, or at least the vast majority of the ones we've tried, they sort of represent these concepts uniquely across contexts.
turns.zh: 就像「哦，得州的首府，那是奥斯汀」。它们几乎对所有东西都有这样的表示——你能想到的每个概念，或者至少我们试过的绝大多数概念，它们会以某种方式在不同语境里表示这些概念。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So one thing I find really neat is there's this debate about our language models thinking, and then that's a hard question, but one aspect of thought is having unique representations that are shared when you think about different things.
turns.zh: 我觉得特别有意思的一点是：外面一直在争论语言模型到底会不会「思考」，这本身很难，但思考的一个面向是：拥有独特的表示，并在思考不同事物时共享这些表示。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So you know what the concept of an I is, and it could be an I in a photo or an I in a medical diagram or an I in a little drawing. And we see that in language models as well.
turns.zh: 比如你知道「字母 I」这个概念，它可以是一张照片里的 I，也可以是医学示意图里的 I，也可以是小小画稿里的 I。我们在语言模型里也看到了这一点。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: If you pass a prompt that has a photo of an I, or you talk about Is in any language, or you draw a little SVG with an I in it and you look at the intermediate results inside the model, the same direction lights up and that direction is like, "Oh, this is an I." And so there's a sense in which they have these general concepts that they know about and that they use and reuse to solve problems.
turns.zh: 你喂进一段带字母 I 的照片，或者用任何语言谈论 I，或者画一个里面含 I 的小 SVG，然后去看模型内部的中间结果，同一个方向会亮起来，那个方向就是「哦，这是字母 I」。所以某种意义上，它们拥有这些通用概念，知道它们、反复用它们来解决问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Another thing that is surprising to people, it's kind of the mirror of what I was saying about I'm saying the sentence saying one word at a time, but I have some destination in mind.
turns.zh: 还有一点也让人意外，它正好是我刚才说的「一次说一个词，但心里有个目的地」的镜像。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So one mystery of language models is, man, if they're outputting only one word at a time, how is it even possible that they could write a coherent report or write code well?
turns.zh: 语言模型有个谜团：天哪，如果它一次只吐出一个词，怎么可能写出一份通顺的报告，或者把代码写好？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: No one on earth that is doing this as their job that's writing reports or writing emails is literally just only thinking about the next word and sentence with no idea, empty mind about anything that comes next. And so that was sort of a big question that we had for a while.
turns.zh: 而现实中，那些以此为职业、每天写报告、写邮件的人，没有一个是真的只在想下一个词、对后面发生什么完全没有想法、脑子里一片空白。所以这曾经是我们心里很大的一个问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And if you look inside these models, one neat fact about these models is that all of the intermediate results that they've produced when they were predicting a word, let's say the fifth word that they predicted, they can be reused. It can be accessed and reused by all of the future words. So what does that mean?
turns.zh: 往这些模型内部看，有件挺妙的事：它在预测某个词（比如预测第五个词）时产生的所有中间结果，都可以被复用——后续的每一个词都能访问并复用它们。这意味着什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: That means that in practice, we find that models will, in their intermediate results, sometimes formulate a plan. The example we have for this is poetry. It's hard to rhyme without planning. You kind of have to think of like, "Oh, I just ended my first rhyme in a it word, and so I should end my second line with another it word.
turns.zh: 意味着在实践中我们发现，模型有时会在中间结果里拟出一个计划。我们手上的例子是写诗——不押韵就很难写，你多少得先想：「哦，我刚用了个以 it 结尾的韵脚，那第二行我大概也该用另一个 it 结尾的词」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Maybe the word I should end it with is rabbit." And we find that if you look at models as they're writing poetry, you see exactly that. They write a line and then in their intermediate results, they're like, "Oh, oh, oh, this is an it rhyme. I should rhyme with rabbit." And then every future word that they predict looks back to that plan they made.
turns.zh: 也许是「rabbit」这个词。而我们发现，看着模型写诗的时候，中间结果里确实就是这样：它写完一行，然后中间结果里冒出「哦哦哦，这是 it 韵，我该跟 rabbit 押韵」，之后它预测的每一个未来单词都会回头看这个已经定下的计划。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so even though they're outputting one word at a time, just like I am right now, they can of course have a plan that they follow over many, many, many, many words.
turns.zh: 所以尽管它一次只吐一个词，跟我现在一样，它当然可以有一个计划，并且沿着这个计划走上很多很多很多个词。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so all of a sudden, even though you have a next word predictor, even though it's technically right, you actually have something that's closer to being able to just do higher order tasks where it's like, oh, well, you just have a plan and you just refer back to your plan and you're slowly executing on it. And you can do that without saying the plan.
turns.zh: 于是突然之间，尽管技术上你拥有的仍是一个「下一个词预测器」，你实际拥有的东西却更接近能直接做更高阶的任务：哦，你手上有一份计划，你不断回看计划、慢慢执行它，而且你可以不把这个计划说出口。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: That's the cool part is this plan that we find is in these intermediate results inside the model, but the model doesn't even have to say it out loud.
turns.zh: 这里最酷的地方是：我们找到的这份计划存在于模型内部的中间结果里，而模型根本不必把它讲出来。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Wow. I know that this is exactly what you described as one of the biggest findings you guys have discovered about how AI thinks, this kind of assumption we all... It was originally built, the original idea of how LLMs operate was this next token predictor. And you're saying that that's not actually how it is anymore. They plan, they think ahead.
turns.zh: 哇。我知道，这正是你描述的你们关于 AI 如何思考的最大发现之一。我们所有人都抱着这样一种假设……LLM 最初被造出来时，关于它怎么运作的原始想法就是「下一个词预测器」。而你说现在其实不是这样了。它们会计划，会提前思考。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: It's not just, like you said, this idea of an empty mind picking the next word independent of everything else.
turns.zh: 不是你说的那种「空白的大脑独立地挑下一个词，跟别的一切无关」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: That's right. And I think those two visions actually aren't as in conflict as you'd think in that you train the model by asking it to be like, "Hey, what happens next? What's next? What happens next?
turns.zh: 没错。而且我觉得这两种图景其实没有你想的那么冲突。因为你训练模型的方式，就是不停地问它：「接下来会怎样？接下来是什么？接下来会怎样？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: What happens next?" And then if you do that and the model gets good enough and you give it hard enough tasks, well, then of course the best way to know what happens next is to think about what happens way down the line. You can think of even in this pre-training phase when the models are reading a story with characters and it's like, oh, what is this character going to do next?
turns.zh: 接下来会怎样？」而如果你这么训练，模型足够强、你给的任务足够难，那当然最好的办法就是去想很久以后会发生什么。你甚至可以想象在预训练阶段，模型在读一个有角色的故事，它在想：这个角色接下来会做什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Well, the best way to know that is to be like, okay, so this character is generally in love with that character and they've been planning to declare their love at this instant or in the future. And so to do that, they probably should do this thing. And so what they're going to say is that.
turns.zh: 那么最好的办法就是：好，这个角色总体上是爱着另一个角色的，而且他们一直在盘算着在这个时刻或将来某刻表明心意。所以为了做成这件事，他大概应该做这个动作。所以他要说的就是这个。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so even though you're only predicting the next instant, it's like, yeah, but to do that really well, you have to have a really good understanding of what's going on, including what you think might happen in the future.
turns.zh: 所以尽管你只是在预测下一个瞬间，但要把这件事做好，你必须对正在发生什么有很好的理解，包括你推测的未来会怎样。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's so interesting about this is how you have to kind of peek inside its little thought process. As a consumer of AI, you kind of give it a prompt and then you wait for it to say something. And what you look at is something that happens between those two where it kind of thinks. Talk a little bit about what that little space is, how you're able to observe these sorts of things.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，你得往它那个小小的思考过程里偷看。作为 AI 的使用者，你给一个提示，然后等它说点什么。而你看到的，是这两者之间发生的、它「思考」的那一小段空间。能不能讲讲这段空间具体是什么，以及你们怎么观察这类东西？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So the right mental model is, again, in between each word, there's multiple steps of computation and in between each steps there's some intermediate result. And what is that result concretely?
turns.zh: 正确的心智模型是：每个词之间有多步计算，每一步之间又会有一些中间结果。那个结果具体是什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's a list of numbers because all these models do is just do a lot of mathematical operations on many numbers. And so initially, if you look at it, it makes no sense. You just have a list of a hundred numbers. The model's doing math.
turns.zh: 就是一串数字，因为这些模型所做的，就是对很多数字做大量数学运算。所以一开始你去看它，根本看不出意义——你只拿到一百个数字，模型在做数学。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's like you look in the middle and there's a hundred random numbers and then the model's writing poetry and there's a hundred numbers and maybe they kind of look different, but it's unclear if they mean anything. And so part of the job is we sort of decode this sort of list of numbers and we try to see if there's structure in it.
turns.zh: 就像你往中间一看是一百个随机数字，模型在写诗时又是一百个数字，也许看起来有点不一样，但它们有没有意义并不清楚。于是工作的一部分就是解码这串数字，看里面有没有结构。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And if you do this very quickly, you realize that there is structure in it. So one common technique that is used in interpretability is you pass a bunch of texts, just all of the texts that you can find, it's just random text through the model, and you record these intermediate numbers for every example, you just record it.
turns.zh: 而你很快就会发现里面确实有结构。可解释性里一个常用手法是：你把一大堆文本——就是你找得到的各种乱七八糟的文本——过一遍模型，把每个样本的这些中间数字都记录下来。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then you just try to see if there's patterns. Are there numbers or pairs of numbers or specific series of numbers that only occur when the model is processing English text or French text or text about love or text about eyes? Or whatever.
turns.zh: 然后你试着找规律：有没有哪些数字、哪些数字对、或者某组特定的数字序列，只在模型处理英文文本、处理法语文本、处理关于爱的文本、处理关于「我」的文本时才出现？诸如此类。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And I think of this as the equivalent of scan my brain and put images in front of me and record everything that activates in my brain as I watch a bunch of images and then be like, "Oh, it seems like when you see images of a house, this part of your brain lights up, but when you see images of a dog, that part of your brain lights up." So that's basically one of the ways that we do what we do.
turns.zh: 我把它类比成：给我大脑做个扫描，把一堆图片摆在我面前，记录我看这些图片时大脑里被激活的一切，然后说「哦，看来你看到房子的图片时，大脑这块亮起来；看到狗的图片时，那块亮起来」。我们做的事基本就是这个。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And if you do it, you do find basically that there's intermediate results that represent all of these concepts that you expect. And so that's the first phase, we decode these intermediate results and now we have a guess as to what they mean, and then we can do a bunch of experiments. We can ask it harder questions and then just label all of the intermediate states and see like, oh, this is what it's doing.
turns.zh: 而你真做了，就会发现确实存在表示这些概念的中间结果。于是第一阶段就完成了：我们解码出这些中间结果，对它们的意思有了个猜测，接下来就能做一堆实验。我们可以问它更难的问题，把所有中间状态都标上标签，然后看出「哦，它原来在做这个」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Or you can even go inside its activations and change it and then see, oh, what would happen if while the model is writing these intermediate results, I went and secretly changed one of the results, and does that do what I would expect? And in fact, oftentimes it does.
turns.zh: 你甚至可以钻进它的激活值里改一下，然后看会怎样：哦，如果模型在写这些中间结果时，我偷偷改了其中一个，会发生什么？它会不会符合我的预期？实际上很多时候，确实会。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: It's so interesting hearing you talk about this and how much of this is us just trying to figure out what the hell is going on versus we designed it this certain way and just how much of this has emerged. I don't know. I guess that's just what makes this such a fun job I imagine for you, just like what is going on? How is this all working?
turns.zh: 听你讲这些特别有意思：这里面有多少是我们在拼命想搞明白到底怎么回事，有多少是「我们本来就这么设计的」，又有多少其实是自己涌现出来的。我不知道。我想这大概就是这份工作对你来说有意思的地方：到底在发生什么？这一切是怎么运作的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, it's a fun and sci-fi job because I have been working in tech for a while and before this I was working on more applied machine learning, and there a lot of what you do is about building systems and it's the practice of software engineering.
turns.zh: 对，这是一份有趣又很科幻的工作。我在科技行业待了一段时间，在这之前做的是更偏应用的机器学习，那时候你做的很多事是搭系统，那是软件工程的训练。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And here a lot of what we do feels so much closer to biology than to engineering because it's just the system arrives at you and you're being asked to say, "Well, we've noticed that Claude can translate words or it can code in this way," or sometimes there's a weird behavior and you're just asked to answer, well, why is it doing that?
turns.zh: 但在这里，我们做的很多事感觉离生物学远得多，离工程学反而更远。因为系统就那么出现在你面前，然后有人问你：「我们发现 Claude 会这样翻译、这样写代码」，或者有时候出现一种奇怪的行为，就让你回答：它为什么要这么做？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: But you don't have access to the source code really like you do for a program. The source code is just this massive list of mathematical operations, which is just incomprehensible.
turns.zh: 但你没法像看一个程序那样拿到源代码。源代码就是一大堆数学运算，根本读不懂。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so you end up in the position of someone kind of similar to someone being asked like, "Hey, when a mouse gets hungry, it sort of gets aggressive, what's going on with that?" And it's like, "Well, I guess I'll run some experiments to see what the factors are." And so it's a very different kind of study than anything that I think most of us on the team have done before.
turns.zh: 所以你的处境就有点像有人问你：「嘿，老鼠一饿就变得有攻击性，这是怎么回事？」你只能说：「好吧，我猜我得做些实验，看看有哪些因素在起作用。」这跟我们团队里大多数人在此之前做过的研究，是完全不同的类型。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah. I imagine people are starting on this, they didn't expect to create this new kind of almost life type of being. Do you think about consciousness as a part of this? Just do you think AI is conscious? Do you think it'll get to a place where we think it's conscious or is that just not even worth our time to think about?
turns.zh: 对。我想象得到，人们一开始做这件事时，并没预料到自己会创造出这么一种近乎生命的存在。你会把意识纳入考虑吗？你觉得 AI 有意识吗？你觉得它会不会走到我们认为它有意识的那一步，还是说这根本不值得我们花时间想？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I mean, I think it's sort of very hard to say one way or another. Some of the most interesting ways to get at this question is interpretability because you're not biased by what the model says.
turns.zh: 我觉得这很难说清是哪一边。其中最有意思的切入方式之一就是可解释性，因为这样你不会被模型自己说的话带偏。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: You can just look at the structure inside and try to determine whether it pushes one way or another on the question.
turns.zh: 你只要看它内部的结构，试着判断在这个问题上它到底偏向哪一边。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I will say that the thing I believe pretty strongly is that most people underestimate the sort of complexity that emerges and that if you look inside, there's just the fact that the models learn these representations for all of the concepts that we have and that we know, that they manipulate them to solve problems, that they do so by planning many tokens ahead, that they sort of have this mix between this higher order reasoning and lower reasoning.
turns.zh: 有一点我相当确信：大多数人低估了涌现出来的那种复杂性。你往里看，就会发现模型为我们已知的所有概念学到了这些表示，会摆弄它们来解决问题，而且是通过提前规划很多个 token 来做的——它算是高阶推理和较低阶推理的一种混合。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And that all of that just kind of emerges is something that I think is underappreciated by people and to me gives me, let's say, a deeper sense of like, "Ooh, there's a lot to still understand about how they work." I think maybe that's the main thing is I find that the more you look inside, the less certain you are about how they work.
turns.zh: 而这一切都是自己涌现出来的，我觉得人们对这点重视不足。对我来说，它带来的是一种更深的感觉：「哦，关于它们怎么运作，还有太多东西需要理解。」我觉得最主要的可能就是：你越往里看，就越不确定它们是怎么运作的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then oftentimes people that will confidently say, "Ah, language models are just X or just Y," are the people that actually haven't spent a while looking inside.
turns.zh: 而那些张口就说「语言模型不过就是 X 或者 Y」的人，往往恰恰是没有花时间往里看过的人。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And there's this, I don't know, thread of history through to how we got here, which is a lot of people did not think we would get to artificial intelligence that is useful by just investing in something that was seemingly very simple and just giving it a lot of compute. And that was famously something OpenAI bet on and then the Anthropic founders were at OpenAI and then spun off, started their own thing.
turns.zh: 这里有一条历史线索通向今天：很多人当初并不认为，只往一个看起来极其简单的东西上砸算力，就能得到有用的 AI。这正是 OpenAI 名义上的那次押注，而 Anthropic 的创始人当时在 OpenAI，后来出走自己创业。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And it was all kind of bet on this bet that, okay, we could just do this seemingly simple thing and give it a ton of compute and it will become incredibly smart. And a lot of people didn't think that was possible and they were proven wrong. So I don't know. Is there anything there that is just like, oh wow, look at this, it worked out?
turns.zh: 他们押的就是这个：好，我们只要做这个看起来很简单的事，给它海量算力，它就会变得极其聪明。很多人觉得不可能，结果他们被证明是错的。所以我想问，这里面有没有什么是你会说「哇，看这个，它真的成了」的地方？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think it's two things actually, because I think it's not just compute, it's also finding an objective where compute keeps giving you returns. So what does that mean? It's actually not that new of an idea.
turns.zh: 我觉得其实是两件事，因为不只是算力，还包括找到一个「算力能持续带来回报」的目标。这是什么意思？其实这不算什么新想法。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I mean, you're right, compute versus sort of, I would say, expert design architectures is a long debate, but then there's an additional step there, which is compute to do what? So there's a bunch of prior work on like, oh, you can spend a bunch of compute to make a bot that's really good at go or that can win some video game.
turns.zh: 你说得对，算力对比我会说的「专家设计的架构」，这是个老争论了。但这上面其实还多一层：算力用来干什么？之前已经有不少工作，比如「你可以花一大笔算力造出一个下围棋很厉害的机器人，或者能赢某个电子游戏的机器人」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then that's cool. And just the fact that that works is sort of interesting, but that doesn't give you something that is nearly as useful as LLMs like Claude are.
turns.zh: 那确实很酷，光是这事能成立本身就挺有意思。但它给不了你一个像 Claude 这样的 LLM 那么有用的东西。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so I think one key thing that many in the field, including me, underappreciated a few years ago and that has borne out, is the combination of compute and the richness of text is what gets you there.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，这几年包括我在内的很多圈内人低估了一件事，而它后来被证明是对的：算力加上文本的丰富性，二者结合才是让你走到今天的原因。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And to me, this is kind of what I was alluding to, but if you think about there's this observation that OpenAI people made, it was a lot of the early team at Anthropic on the scaling loss paper.
turns.zh: 对我来说，这大概就是我刚才想说的意思。但你如果想想，OpenAI 那边的人有一个观察——那篇 scaling loss 论文里，Anthropic 早期团队有不少人参与。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so this is the observation that if you pour in more compute and more data to the task of predicting the next word, you see that the skill of the model you get at predicting the next word just predictably keeps improving. And it's a trend that just keeps going and keeps going and keeps going. And it's an empirical law.
turns.zh: 这个观察是：如果你往「预测下一个词」这件事上灌入更多算力和更多数据，你得到的模型在预测下一个词这件事上的水平，就会可预测地持续变强。这条趋势一直走下去、一直走下去、一直走下去。它是一条经验规律。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: People sort of speculated as to why at the time, but it's sort of still just mostly an empirical finding. And that means that it's like, ah, this is a field where you can just keep pouring more compute and you keep improving on that metric. And that's rare. And also it's rare for it to be a metric that then correlates with a bunch of tasks that we actually care about.
turns.zh: 当时人们也猜测过为什么会这样，但到现在它基本仍然只是一条经验发现。它的意义在于：啊，这是一个你只要继续灌算力、就在这个指标上持续进步的领域。这种事很少见。而更少见的是，这个指标居然还跟你真正在意的一堆任务相关。

With DX, you can measure and benchmark the impact of AI adoption across your full product life cycle. DX shows you where AI is helping developers and where it's creating new bottlenecks.
turns.zh: 本季的支持赞助商是 DX。现在你们公司里每个人终于都在用 AI 了，工程负责人面对的问题不再是「我们在用 AI 吗」，而是「它带来回报了吗」。借助 DX，你可以在整个产品生命周期里衡量并对标 AI 落地的影响。DX 会告诉你 AI 在哪些地方帮到了开发者，又在哪些地方制造了新的瓶颈。
