turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Externally, there's been these kind of big jumps seemingly in what AI can do for us. There was, I forget which version of Opus, where it just unlocked coding. And now as Boris Cherny famously said, "Coding is solved." And many people are just like, "Holy shit." Over I think winter break, we're just like, "Wow, AI is really, really good at this now." So there's been these moments of big jumps in abilities.
turns.zh: 从外面看，AI 能帮我们做的事好像总是出现这种巨大的跳变。我记不清是哪个版本的 Opus，突然就把编程给解锁了。现在就像 Boris Cherny 说的那句名言：「编程已经解决了。」很多人的反应是：「我靠。」我记得去年冬天假期那会儿，我们的感觉是「哇，AI 现在真的、真的已经很擅长这个了」。所以确实出现过这种能力大跳变的时刻。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And you actually said internally, as you just said, it's actually been this very smooth progression of AI power that happens to cross some threshold where now we can do something. Speak a little bit about that.
turns.zh: 而你刚才说，你们内部看到的其实是一路非常平滑的能力提升，只是恰好跨过了某个阈值，于是我们突然能做某件事了。讲讲这个吧。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's a term for this which is sort of this idea of emergence, which is it seems like two things are true at once. There's this predictably smooth trend. And then before Opus 4.5, I really couldn't let Claude cook too much on my code without a short leash. And then after Opus 4.5, I could. And so that's weird.
turns.zh: 这有个专门的说法，叫「涌现」。它看上去是两件事同时成立：一方面是那条可预测的平滑趋势；另一方面，在 Opus 4.5 之前，我实在不敢让 Claude 在我的代码上放开手脚，得一直拽着绳子；到了 Opus 4.5 之后，我就可以放手了。这就很奇怪。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I feel like you would expect a more gradual transition. And the mental model I have for this is there's kind of two ways of looking at it.
turns.zh: 你本会预期是个更渐进的过渡。我对这件事的心智模型是，有两种看它的方式。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So there's the way that I talked about briefly just earlier where it's like, if you're just doing this kind of next token prediction, you could imagine that all the text in the world has easy words and medium words and hard words in terms of how hard they are to predict.
turns.zh: 一种是我前面简单提过的：如果你只是在做这种下一个 token 预测，你可以想象全世界所有的词，按预测难度分成易词、中等词和难词。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so as you're going down this curve, first, the model is bad at everything, and then at some point it gets all of the easy words right. And that means maybe the easy words are the structure of sentences. And so the model all of a sudden can write coherent sentences, but just one sentence at a time. And so it's kind of cool and impressive, but we can't really do anything with that.
turns.zh: 于是随着你沿着这条曲线往下走，一开始模型什么都做不好；到某个点，它把所有易词都答对了。这意味着易词可能就是句子的结构。于是模型突然能写出通顺的句子，但一次只能写一句。这挺酷、挺让人印象深刻的，可我们拿它做不了什么。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then maybe the medium words are these basic facts about the world. And as the model smoothly gets better at predicting words, at some point it predicts most of the medium words right. And now all of a sudden it can write coherent sentences and sentences that are true. And so now maybe it's helpful to write emails. Maybe it's helpful to help you write drafts of blog posts.
turns.zh: 然后中等词可能是关于世界的基本事实。随着模型平滑地变得更会预测词，到某个点它把大部分中等词都预测对了。于是它突然能写出既通顺又为真的句子。这时它可能就有用来写邮件了，可能就有用来帮你起草博客了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Even though that was a smooth improvement, it just takes it taking over to be helpful. And then I guess the hard words, which maybe are your domain expertise, like science or code. And another way to look at it is it's a question of how many of these words do you get right and how many do you get wrong?
turns.zh: 虽然这是个平滑的改进，但要「越过那条线」它才真正变得有用。再往后就是难词了，那可能就是你的专业领域，比如科学或者代码。另一种看法是：这是个「你答对了多少、又答错了多少」的问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Once you get to the point where you're getting, I don't know, maybe 90% of the medium words right, then you're useful as an email writer. But if you're at 50%, it's actually wasting my time to use you because I'm just going to have to go in and fix it half the time.
turns.zh: 当你达到某个点，比如中等词能答对 90%，那你当个写邮件的助手就有用了。但如果只有 50%，用它其实是在浪费我的时间，因为一半的时候我还是得进去改。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: But if I have to go in and fix it 10% of the time, it's better, or 5% of the time, it's better. Different tasks have different reliability thresholds, but you smoothly improve and then at some point it's just reliable enough to be good.
turns.zh: 但如果我只需要 10% 的时候进去改，那就更好了；5% 的时候更好。不同任务有不同的可靠性门槛，而你是平滑地变强，然后到某个点就「足够可靠、于是够用了」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And again, for me, my lived experience is basically exactly that, which is that at some point I was just using the models to help when I was stuck. I would just talk to them and then they would never write my code. And then at some point they could write small snippets of code basically all the time. So now I don't write small snippets.
turns.zh: 对我来说，我的亲身经历基本就是这样：一开始我只是卡住了才去问模型，跟它们聊完，它们从来不会帮我写代码。然后到某个点，它们基本一直能写小段代码，于是现在小段代码我不写了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And at some point, they could write large snippets. This year, basically Claude has taken on most of my code writing and that's because it went from doing that correctly, I don't know, 80% of the time, which was not useful, to 99% of the time, which now is useful.
turns.zh: 再后来，它们能写大段代码。今年基本上 Claude 接手了我大部分的代码写作，这就是因为它从「大概 80% 的时候写对」，那还没法用，变成了「99% 的时候写对」，现在就有用了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so this combination of smooth improvement and then each different task has a different threshold at which now it becomes solved, I think gives you these big jumps even though we're just smoothly going down that scale.
turns.zh: 所以我认为：平滑的改进，加上每类任务各有各的「过了这条线就算解决」的阈值，就给了你这些巨大的跳变——尽管我们其实只是在沿着那把尺子平滑地往下走。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I think this is really interesting, this idea that the models are just smoothly getting smarter, but once they hit some threshold of they're this often good at this thing, it changes the world. Because I think internally you would think it'd be like, oh wow, this next model is crazy, so much different.
turns.zh: 我觉得这个想法特别有意思：模型只是一直平滑地变聪明，但一旦它在某件事上「好到这个程度」的阈值被跨过，世界就变了。因为按理说，内部会觉得「哇，这个新模型太不一样了，差别好大」。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: But it's like, no, okay, you can almost predict, give it these many GPUs, this much data, it's going to get this smart. And it may not be obvious exactly what will change and what unlocks, but I know another part of it is just the data you feed it. There's all this RL work and all this specific data that you train it on, become a better writer, become better at math. I imagine it's part of it too. Okay.
turns.zh: 但其实不是。好吧，你几乎可以预测：给它这么多 GPU、这么多数据，它就会变这么聪明。具体会发生什么变化、什么被解锁，未必明显，但我知道另一个原因是它吃进去的数据——还有大量的强化学习工作，以及专门喂给它的那些数据，让它更会写、 更擅长数学。我想这也是其中一部分。好。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So one of the big questions I think on people's minds these days, a big debate happening is just AI doing bad things, the potential damage it can do because as it gets smarter, and it's been doing bad things. There's been bad things happening recently.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得如今大家心里最大的一个问题、正在发生的最大一场辩论，就是 AI 干坏事——它越来越聪明之后可能造成的破坏。最近确实出了一些不好的事。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So a big question for you is just as someone that watches these models think and operate, why is it so hard to catch it thinking badly, trying to deceive us, and do something bad? Why is that not just a solution to the problem of AI alignment?
turns.zh: 所以想问你一个大问题：作为一个天天看着这些模型怎么思考、怎么运转的人，为什么这么难发现它心里在想坏主意、想骗我们、想干坏事？为什么这本身不就是 AI 对齐问题的一个解法吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: In one sense, it's totally the solution. You watch it and you catch if it does bad stuff. So I think there's tiers to this. So I would think of maybe one part of it is pure engineering.
turns.zh: 从某种意义上说，它完全是解法。你盯着它，就能抓住它干坏事的时候。我觉得这件事是分层的。一部分算是纯粹的工程问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's like, well, you're giving access to the model to certain things and certain things should be off limits. In some contexts, it shouldn't have access to the internet. In some contexts, it should only have access to a small narrow piece of your computer, stuff like that. So that's one part of the work and that's helpful.
turns.zh: 比如，你给模型开放某些东西的权限，而某些东西就应该禁止碰。在某些场景下，它不该有互联网访问权；在某些场景下，它只该能访问你电脑上很小的一块特定区域，诸如此类。这是工作的一部分，而且很有用。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: But then there's two additional things that I think are squishier and harder and that we focus on more. So interp is part of alignments and broadly I think of two big goals.
turns.zh: 但另外还有两件事更「软」、更难，也是我们投入更多的。所以可解释性是对齐的一部分，宏观上我认为有两个大目标。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's many more, but two that are important I think to understand is you want to generally understand how the model behaves, what kind of thing is it? What are its propensities? Does it tend to do X when put in Y situation? And if so, why?
turns.zh: 当然还有很多别的，但有两个我觉得很重要、需要理解：一个是你要总体上搞清楚这个模型怎么表现、它是个什么东西、它有哪些倾向？被放进 Y 情形里时，它是不是倾向于做 X？如果是，为什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Is it the case that the model will only behave well when it has some evidence that it's being observed and monitored, that it's in some evaluation? And then if it doesn't have that evidence, that it'll behave poorly.
turns.zh: 会不会存在这种情况：模型只在有证据表明自己正被观察、被监控、正处在某种评估里的时候才表现良好；而如果没有这类证据，它就会表现糟糕？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So there's this generally characterizing what kind of thing you're interacting with because then it's just like anything in security, you need to have a mental model of what's the risk? What can they do? What do they tend to do? And so this is broader character training.
turns.zh: 所以要先总体刻画清楚你正在打交道的到底是个什么东西，因为这样一来就和安全领域一样：你得对风险有个心理模型——它能做什么？它通常会做什么？所以这就是更广义的品格训练。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We've talked about the constitution and the docs where we explicitly want to shape the character of Claude, for example, of what kind of behavior should it be okay doing? And that's the goal. But then the role of interpreting other parts of alignment is then trying to see, well, did that work?
turns.zh: 我们谈到过的 constitution 和那些文档，就是我们明确想要塑造 Claude 的品格：什么样的行为它应该做、做了才算可以。这就是目标。而可解释性在对齐里的另一个作用，则是去检验：好，这真的有效吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We trained Claude to be helpful, harmless and honest and we can look inside and see is it or is it the case that it's behaving well, but if you look inside actually it's like, "Oh, I'm only behaving well because Lenny's watching right now," and if you weren't, it would do something else.
turns.zh: 我们把 Claude 训练成有帮助、无害、诚实的，而我们可以往里看：它到底是表现良好，还是说往里看会发现「哦，我只是因为 Lenny 在看着才表现良好」，你要是不看着，它就会做别的事。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So there's this sort of trying to understand what kind of behavior we formed and trying to mold it and trying to check that we've molded the right way. And then the second part is this sort of, well, yeah, just observe the model and see if it's doing bad stuff. For the basics of that, you don't necessarily need interp.
turns.zh: 所以这里有一件事是：试图理解我们塑造出了什么样的行为，努力去塑造它，再检查我们塑得对不对。第二部分则是：好，那就观察这个模型，看它有没有干坏事。对这件事的基本盘，你其实不一定需要可解释性。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: You can just have another language model read transcripts and be like, "Hey, did this model do anything bad here?" And stop it. But you can also use interp to try to get at parts that are these unverbalized parts, these parts that only exist in these intermediate results. Models are able to represent stuff in their intermediate results that they don't say as we've established.
turns.zh: 你完全可以让另一个语言模型去读这些对话记录，然后问：「嘿，这个模型在这里干坏事了没有？」然后叫停它。但你也可以用可解释性，去够那些没法用语言表达的部分，那些只存在于中间结果里的部分。正如我们前面确认过的，模型能在中间结果里表示一些它从不说出口的东西。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so one of the roles of interp is to try to identify cases when this happens and prevents them. And then one thing that my team works on that I think is along those lines is kind of a fun bit of alignment as I think of it as almost being maybe not a PI, but they're investigations or deep dives.
turns.zh: 所以可解释性的一个作用，就是试着识别出这种情况并加以防范。我团队做的另一件事，我觉得也属于这个方向，按我的说法更像是一段有趣的「对齐工作」——算是调查或者说深度排查。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We'll see a model do something really weird and really perplexed by it and we'll try to understand what happened. So a recent example of this is there was this model we were training and sometimes in math problems, it would go crazy.
turns.zh: 我们看到模型做出非常古怪的行为，百思不得其解，就试着去弄明白发生了什么。最近的一个例子是：我们当时在训练的一个模型，它在做数学题时有时会突然发疯。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It would do some math, it would get to an answer, I think it was 12, and then it would immediately go back and say, "Oh no, oh my God, the answer actually is for sure 36. I should say 36." And they would do math again, it would get to 12. And then immediately it would say, "No, actually the answer should be 36." And slowly it would start descending into madness, writing in all caps, literally saying, "I'm possessed by a demon." And you're like, "What is going on?
turns.zh: 它算一些数学，得出一个答案，我记得是 12，然后立刻回头说：「哦不，天哪，答案肯定是 36。我应该说 36。」然后它再算一遍，又得到 12，接着马上说：「不，其实答案应该是 36。」它慢慢滑向疯狂，开始全大写地写字，字面意义上说：「我被恶魔附身了。」你就会想：到底怎么回事？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Why is it losing its mind here?" And if you look inside, again, these intermediate results at what's going on in this example, you'll see that over the prompts that just described the math problem, before the model even did anything, there was a huge intermediate result activation for 36.
turns.zh: 它怎么在这里失去了理智？而如果你往里看，再看这个例子里的中间结果，你会看到：在那些只是描述了数学题的提示上，在模型还没做任何事之前，就已经有了一个指向「36」的巨大中间结果激活。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The model's already obsessed with the number 36 before it's even had a chance to understand what the problem is. And what was happening is that the model was able to do math correctly, the answer correctly was 12, but it had been trained by accident on similar questions where the answer was incorrectly marked as 36.
turns.zh: 模型在还没机会理解题目是什么之前，就已经 obsessed 上「36」这个数字了。原因是：模型其实能正确做数学、正确答案是 12，但它曾经被意外地用相似题目训练过，而那些题目的答案被错误地标注成了 36。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so the model knew that the correct answer was 12, and it also had been optimized to say 36. It had this pressure of saying 36 because that's what had been rewarded. And so it was sort of going haywire just because it had memorized this result.
turns.zh: 于是模型知道正确答案是 12，同时它又被优化成「说 36」——因为那才是被奖励过的。它身上有一种说 36 的压力。所以它基本上是因为记住了这个结果而变得失控。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's like you see this weird behavior and you look inside and you try to see if what you find inside can help you understand what's going on so that you can improve the general alignment of this model and future models.
turns.zh: 你看到一个古怪的行为，往里看，试图看看里面的东西能不能帮你理解发生了什么，从而改进这个模型以及未来模型的整体对齐。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Along those lines, there was famously the Golden Gate Claude, which was just obsessed with the Golden Gate and every answer and find some way to reference the Golden Gate Bridge.
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，有那个很有名的「Golden Gate Claude」，它痴迷于金门大桥，每个回答都要想办法扯到金门大桥上。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yes, yes. Well, that one was an interp experiment. So the cool part of that one is we just found the intermediate results that matched the Golden Gate, and usually it's only on when the model talks about the Golden Gate, but we just turned it on always.
turns.zh: 对，对。那个其实是一次可解释性实验。酷的地方在于，我们找到了那些对应「金门」的中间结果；它通常只在模型谈到金门时才被激活，而我们把它设成了永远开启。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Always. Super intentional to see what would happen.
turns.zh: 永远开启。非常刻意，就是想看看会发生什么。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Well, yeah. And it's also one way that you convince yourself that you found the right thing. How do you know for sure that this thing we decoded that we think is the Golden Gate sign is actually the Golden Gate thing? It's like turn it on always and see if the model behaves like that. And it did.
turns.zh: 对。而且这也是一种说服自己「找对了东西」的方式：你怎么确定我们解码出来的、我们认为是金门大桥这个概念的中间结果，真的就是金门大桥？办法就是把它永远打开，看看模型是不是表现出相应的行为。结果是的。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So funny. So coming back to this alignment stuff, so this is interesting. So your org is under the AI alignment org and just thinking through how it takes to align AI to do things we want, what were the three components that you describe? Honest, what are the...
turns.zh: 真有意思。回到对齐这个话题，你的部门在对齐团队下面，思考的是怎么把 AI 对齐到我们想要的行为上。你刚才提到的那三个组成部分是什么？老实说，你刚说的那三个是……

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, helpful, harmless, and honest?
turns.zh: 哦，有帮助、无害、诚实？

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Helpful, harmful, and harmless and honest. So there's the train AI to be aligned, and then there's the, okay, let's watch it and see how it operates. Are those the two sides of the coin of how we solve this problem?
turns.zh: 有帮助、无害、诚实。所以一边是「把 AI 训练成对齐的」，另一边是「好，我们盯着它，看它怎么运作」。这就是解决这个问题的硬币两面吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. It's sort of really integrated is how I would describe it.
turns.zh: 对。要说整合到什么程度的话，我会说它们其实是深度整合在一起的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: You can't really separate, have one team that's just like, "Hey, we're the assembly line making Claudes," and another team that's like, "Oh, we looked at them and they're no good." There's this tight loop of we noticed some pattern that's concerning or some behavior that could be improved, and then you immediately change training so that you can improve on it.
turns.zh: 你没法真的拆开：一队人只负责「嘿，我们是生产 Claude 的流水线」，另一队人只负责「哦，我们检查了一下，他们不行」。而是一个紧密的闭环：我们发现某个让人担心的模式、或者某个可以改进的行为，然后立刻去改训练，从而把它改进掉。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Awesome. I feel like Anthropic gets so much flack for this that I feel like is so unfair. Anthropic's, I think, official company name is AI Safety Research Lab, something like that. The reason Anthropic was founded is because they were afraid that people weren't taking safety seriously enough. And then Dario is always out there, "This is really dangerous. We got to be really careful.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得 Anthropic 在这件事上挨了不少很不公平的批评。我觉得 Anthropic 的官方定位大概是「AI 安全研究实验室」之类的。它之所以成立，就是因为他们担心大家对安全不够认真。然后 Dario 总在那儿说「这真的很危险，我们得非常非常小心。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: We got to go really slowly." And everyone's just like, "No, he's just saying that for marketing reasons. He's trying to convince everyone to fund them and all these things." And now it's like, "Wait, shit, it's really dangerous. We got to be really thoughtful about this stuff." I feel like Anthropic's got a lot of unfair criticism for this. I know you guys have been thinking about this for a long time. I don't know. Anything there?
turns.zh: 我们必须走得很慢。」而所有人都是：「不，他不过是为了营销才那么说，他是想说服大家都去资助他们之类的。」现在变成了：「等等，靠，这真的很危险，我们得对这件事非常上心。」我觉得 Anthropic 承受了很多不该承受的批评。我知道你们想这件事已经很久了。有没有什么想说的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: A lot of the actions that certainly the alignment team takes, and I think Anthropic takes, just predicated on take the idea that this technology is going to keep improving seriously, just that's it.
turns.zh: 对齐团队（我敢说 Anthropic 整体）采取的很多行动，前提其实就是同一个：这项技术会持续显著变强。就这一点。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Because if you do, and let's say you rewind the clock back to '25 or something or '24, and you're like, "Hey, I think in a couple years, good chances that Claude can just basically write code as well as a trained software engineer, and a few years later it can write it better than any engineer." There's always uncertainty with this.
turns.zh: 因为如果你认真对待这件事——比如说，我们把时钟拨回 2025 年、或者 2024 年，然后你说：「嘿，我猜再过两三年，Claude 有很大概率能写出跟受过训练的软件工程师一样好的代码；再过几年，它能写得比任何工程师都好。」这里面永远是有不确定性的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: When is it going to happen? How likely? But if you take that seriously, then I think it's just about doing the responsible thing, condition on that worldview. Okay, well, if this is happening, then we should make sure that cybersecurity concerns are addressed and things of that nature. Actually, I think of it as...
turns.zh: 什么时候会发生？概率多大？但如果你认真对待这件事，我觉得就只是「在这个世界观下做负责任的事」：好，如果这事正在发生，那我们就该确保网络安全之类的顾虑被处理掉。我其实把它看成……

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: To me, sometimes this debate is almost... When I feel like people on the other side disagree, it's almost like I feel like, ah, but I think they don't really believe that this technology is going to continue to improve. And then it's true that it's not that scary. And I think empirically, so far, the pace of progress has been passed and showing no sign of slowing down. So I think that's why a lot of the safety work is important to keep doing.
turns.zh: 对我来说，有时候这场争论几乎就是……当我感觉另一边的人不同意时，我心里想的是：啊，我觉得他们其实并不相信这项技术会继续进步。那确实就没那么可怕。而从经验上看，到目前为止，进步的速度已经被证明远超预期，而且没有任何要慢下来的迹象。所以我觉得这就是为什么大量的安全工作值得继续做下去。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's something you think people maybe misunderstand about this AI safety stuff, just what's going on right now? Is there something you're just like, "Come on. Okay, here's what you need to know. Here's something you may be missing."
turns.zh: 关于 AI 安全这件事，你觉得人们可能误解了什么？眼下正在发生的是什么？有没有什么事是你想说「拜托，好吧，这是你该知道的，这是你可能漏掉的一点」？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: This might be a bit of a sidetrack, but my take would be that a lot of the thing that I think people, maybe a little bit outside of the course of AI safety effort or that haven't been steeped in it for as long, react really strongly to, and I think is maybe not super helpful, or at least as worth thinking about more, is this question of anthropomorphization.
turns.zh: 这可能有点跑题，但我的看法是：很多人——可能是不在 AI 安全这条路上浸淫太久、或者没浸淫那么久的人——对它反应特别强烈，而我觉得这件事可能没那么有用，或者至少值得更多想一想的，就是「拟人化」这个问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Should you think of the models as... Should you model the model as something that's closer to some entity or closer to a tool? And I actually think that both are wrong.
turns.zh: 你该把模型看成……你该把建模的对象看成更接近某种「实体」，还是更接近一件「工具」？而我其实认为这两种都不对。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's a sense in which all mental models are wrong, but some are useful. And that in terms of understanding the kind of stuff that happens and predicting the kind of risks that materialize, the anthropomorphization is actually a useful way to talk about LLMs. I have a few reasons why, I hope you'll get into them, but I think that's probably my main take here.
turns.zh: 某种意义上，所有心智模型都是错的，但有些是有用的。而在理解会发生什么、预测哪些风险会真正落地这件事上，拟人化其实是一种谈论 LLM 的好方式。我有几个理由，希望你展开讲讲，不过这大概就是我的主要观点。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah, please share because I know Dwarkesh famously, I don't know, famously put out this whole story of the Hugging Face incident and people criticize them for anthropomorphizing AI. So it's really interesting to hear you would think that's actually a useful way to think about it. Talk more about that.
turns.zh: 请务必讲讲，因为我知道 Dwarkesh 很有名地——至少是很有名地——发过那篇讲 Hugging Face 事件的文章，人们批评他在拟人化 AI。所以听你说这其实是一种有用的思考方式，真的很有意思。再展开说说。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's funny because on a smaller scale, when I worked on showing that LLMs plan ahead, there was some pushback on the term planning, again, because it was sort of like, "Ah, well, can you really say that's something that's just predicting the next token's planning?" And I think there's this kind of semantic debate where you can arbitrarily define terms and then there's just the, what is the terminology that actually describes what is happening?
turns.zh: 这挺好笑，因为在更小的尺度上，我做「证明 LLM 会提前规划」那个工作的时候，就有人对「规划」这个词提出异议，说：「哎，一个只是在预测下一个 token 的东西，你真能说它会『规划』吗？」我觉得这是一种语义层面的争论：你可以任意定义术语，然后就变成「到底哪个词才真正描述了正在发生的事」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: What is the word that actually describes what is happening easily? So here's why I think LLMs plan, but also here's why I think this language that's anthropomorphic can often be really useful. If you think back to what we were saying about how the models are made, first of all, they predict massive amounts of text written by humans. That's the first step.
turns.zh: 到底哪个词能轻松地描述正在发生的事。所以，我下面既讲为什么我认为 LLM 会规划，也讲为什么我认为这种拟人化的语言往往真的很有用。回想我们说过的模型是怎么造出来的：首先，它们预测了人类写下的海量文本。这是第一步。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: As we are learning more and more by looking inside, doing this well requires building up a model of the world, a model of what kind of world generated all of these texts. And we can find that these models are learning these general ideas, these general concepts. So that's one.
turns.zh: 而随着我们往里看得越来越多、把这件事做得越来越好，我们发现做好它需要建立起一个关于世界的模型——一个「什么样的世界生成了这些文本」的模型。而我们能找到，这些模型确实在学到这些通用的想法、通用的概念。这是第一条理由。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So they have an understanding of the world. It's not just a surface level only to text, to understand the process that made the texts. Then there's a second reason, which is that as part of this training, they also encounter millions of dialogues. Predicting the next character in a dialogue requires behaving like the character in the dialogue would.
turns.zh: 所以它们对世界是有理解的，不只是停留在文本表面，而是理解了生成这些文本的过程。第二条理由是：作为训练的一部分，它们还会遇到数百万段对话。预测对话中的下一个字，就要求你表现得像对话里那个角色会表现的那样。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: In that sense, part of their training I think can best be thought as training an actor where it's like it's reading some play and it has to play all sides because it's predicting all the words, and so it has to act as this specific character that was scorned in act one and enacted revenge in act two and is facing the consequences in act three.
turns.zh: 从这个意义上说，我认为它们训练的一部分，最贴切的想法像是「训练一个演员」：它读着一出戏，却必须把所有角色的台词都预测出来，所以它必须演第一幕里被轻蔑的那个角色、第二幕里完成复仇的那个角色、第三幕里承受后果的那个角色。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And to do that well, you need to model what the motivations and the feelings of that character might be. And then another thing that people might not know is when you talk to Claude, when you talk to these assistants, you go to claude.ai, the way that it's formatted to the model is just as a dialogue, as a conversation between you and the model.
turns.zh: 而要把这个演好，你就得建模这个角色的动机和感受是什么。还有一点很多人可能不知道：你跟 Claude 说话、跟这些助手说话的时候，你打开 claude.ai，呈现给模型的形式就是一段对话——你与模型之间的一场对话。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So it literally says, Human: "Hey Claude, help me write this email." And then, Assistant: Claude's answer. Claude is literally in this role playing as a helpful assistant in this dialogue that is much like all of these dialogues that it's been trained on. And there's a third reason.
turns.zh: 它字面上就写着 Human：「嘿 Claude，帮我写这封邮件。」然后 Assistant：Claude 的回答。所以 Claude 真的就在扮演对话里那个乐于助人的角色，而这场对话跟它被训练过的那些对话非常像。这就是第二条理由。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And the third reason is that another part of training that's a big part of training nowadays all around is sort of outcome-oriented tasks where you train the model to be good at coding, for example, and to do that, you just have it do whatever it wants, and then it writes some code, and then you have some program on the other side that just checks if the code is right.
turns.zh: 第三条理由是：训练的另一个部分——如今到处都占很大比重的部分——是那种「以结果为导向」的任务。比如你训练模型把代码写好，办法就是让它随便写，然后另一头有个程序来检查代码对不对。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so the model's just going to have a bunch of optimization pressure to just try to learn a bunch of different strategies to do this well.
turns.zh: 于是模型身上就有一大堆优化压力，促使它去学各种不同的策略来把这件事做好。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And it turns out that some of these strategies materialize in behavior that can look surprisingly human, which isn't that shocking because things like deception, like, "Hey, I can get the reward for this task if I write a program that the program that's verifying it will get fooled by, even though it's not exactly what it is.
turns.zh: 结果是，其中一些策略会表现为看起来惊人地像人的行为。这并不太令人意外，因为像欺骗这类东西，比如「嘿，如果我写一个能骗过检查程序、从而拿到这个任务奖励的程序，我就能拿到奖励，尽管那并不完全是事实。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: If that works, then I will learn to do that." Frustration, "Ha, I've been trying this approach for a while to solve this hard problem. It's not working." So that's an incentive to try something different or surprise. "Oh, I was expecting this to produce this answer, but it didn't.
turns.zh: 如果这样行得通，我就会学会这么做。」还有受挫：「哈，我一直用这个方法解这个难题，已经试了一阵了，不管用。」这就是一种去试别的东西、或者去带来惊喜的激励：「哦，我本以为这会产出这个答案，结果没有。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Maybe I have my mental model a bit wrong." And so as you apply enough pressure on it, and you're starting from this prior of the model already knowing all these concepts, it's going to reinforce the ones that are useful to do all of these tasks.
turns.zh: 也许我对它的心智模型有点不对。」所以当你施加足够的压力，并且你从「模型已经掌握这些概念」这个先验出发时，它就会强化那些对完成这些任务有用的概念。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so what do you get at the end, you get this sort of model that can be a super good simulator or actor of all of these characters and that's been trained to act as a character in dialogues and also to learn behaviors that lead it to complete tasks well.
turns.zh: 所以最后你得到的是这样一个模型：它能当所有这些角色的极好模拟器或演员，被训练成在对话里扮演角色，同时也学会了那些能让它把任务完成好的行为。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The best way to understand how that thing behaves is not exactly like a human, but man, kind of like something that's mimicking a human, is really close, and is much closer than a program. A program is a very predictive thing. This is something else entirely. And so that's why I think it's actually a super useful frame.
turns.zh: 理解这个东西如何表现，最好的方式并不是「它像个人」，而是：天哪，它更像是某种在模仿人类的东西，非常接近，而且比程序近得多。程序是很可预测的东西，这完全是另一回事。所以我觉得这是一个非常有用的框架。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Wow. Oh my God, there's so much interesting stuff there. How often is your mind just kind of blown thinking about basically we've created this alien being that we are now trying to understand what we have created? How often as you watch it just like, "Wow, that's crazy. I didn't expect that."
turns.zh: 哇。天哪，这里面有太多有意思的东西了。想到我们基本上创造出了一个异类存在，而我们现在正在试图理解自己创造了什么——你的脑子有多经常被震到？看着它运转的时候，你有多经常会想「哇，这太离谱了，我没想到」？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, a lot. This is just next token prediction on a bunch of text. It goes against so many of our intuitions. We're like, no, the way that you make an intelligence is you give it lessons, you bring it up, you do all this complicated stuff, and it's like, no, absolutely not.
turns.zh: 经常。这无非就是在一堆文本上做下一个 token 预测。它违背了我们太多直觉。我们会想：不对，制造智能的方式明明是给它上课、把它培养起来、你要做一大堆复杂的事——而事实是：不，绝不是这样。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We do this incredibly simple thing, and yet we're at the point where it's breaking new ground in mathematics. I think if you hold these two thoughts in your head, there's two reactions you can have.
turns.zh: 我们做的是一件极其简单的事，可我们却走到了它在数学上开辟新天地的地步。我觉得如果你同时装着这两个念头，就会有两种反应。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's denial and there's curiosity where denial is just, this is just not possible if all you're doing is predicting the next word, it's not possible that you could ever match the best specialists in our field. And I think that position just gets harder and harder as we get more empirical evidence that actually that is what's happening.
turns.zh: 一种是否认，一种是好奇。否认就是：「如果你做的只是预测下一个词，这根本不可能，你怎么可能达到我们领域最顶尖专家的水平。」而随着越来越多的经验证据表明事情真是这样，这种立场只会越来越站不住脚。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And curiosity is kind of the road I've ended up choosing, which is just like, well, how is this happening? Let's open up. Let's look inside. How could it be that one of the early projects I did at Anthropic is I learned SQL, a programming language, and it took me years to master.
turns.zh: 好奇则是我最终选择的道路，就是：这事到底是怎么发生的？我们打开它，往里看。我早期在 Anthropic 做的项目之一是学 SQL——一门编程语言——我花了好几年才掌握。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then as a little side project, I got Claude to learn SQL and it was better than me at it, and I'll never be better than Claude at SQL ever again. It took it just like this simple process. How could this be? I think there's so much depth in that question and just so much to explore.
turns.zh: 然后我拿它当成个业余项目，让 Claude 去学 SQL，结果它比我还强，而我这辈子在 SQL 上都不可能再超过 Claude 了。它只靠这么简单一个流程就做到了。这怎么可能？那个问题里有太深的可挖之处，也有太多东西可以探索。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And it's to me so fascinating to just every day try to unpack that, try to peel a few layers of the onions back like, okay, well, clearly this is happening. The simple objective is giving rise to this super complicated thing. Okay, let's figure out why. Let's figure out, oh, it's learning these general concepts. Oh, it has these circuits. Oh, okay. What's the next question? What's the next thing we don't know?
turns.zh: 对我来说，每天试着拆解这个、试着把洋葱剥开几层，实在太有意思了：好吧，显然这事正在发生。一个简单的目标，长出了这么复杂的东西。好，那我们来搞清楚为什么。来看看，哦，它在学这些通用概念。哦，它有这些回路。哦，好。那下一个问题是什么？下一个我们不知道的东西是什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And I don't know, my sort of maybe most optimistic take on this is that I think we're going to learn a lot about just the nature of intelligence itself, of how you get this super complex thing that emerges from simple objectives. And in fact, I would argue that we're another example of this.
turns.zh: 我不知道，我可能最乐观的看法是：我认为我们会学到很多关于智能本质本身的东西——关于你是怎么从一个简单的目标里长出这么复杂的东西的。事实上，我会说我们自己就是另一个例子。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Evolution, pretty simple objective. You sort of shake things around for a while and keep the organisms that manage to adapt to the environment, and at the end you get jazz and podcasts. That's kind of crazy as well. And so I think there's a sense in which there's some fundamental truth that we can learn by studying these things.
turns.zh: 进化，一个相当简单的目标。你就是把东西搅和一阵子，保留那些能适应环境的生物，最后你就得到了爵士乐和播客。这也挺疯狂的。所以我觉得，研究这些东西能让我们学到某种根本性的真理。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Wow. Something that comes up as you say that is what's interesting now is AI is helping us learn and progress, like AI tutoring and all these things. It's interesting how it now is helping us accelerate our own understanding of the world.
turns.zh: 哇。你这么说让我想到一件现在很有意思的事：AI 正在帮助我们学习和进步，比如 AI 家教之类的。它现在正在加速我们自己对世界的理解，这很有意思。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And I wonder if this point you made about how the way we learn was lessons, AI is learning just processing a ton of data. I wonder if that's how we end up... I wonder if we change our education system based on what LLMs have been trained on.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，你刚才说我们人类的学习方式是「上课」，而 AI 的学习只是处理海量数据。我有时候会想，我们会不会因此改变教育体系——依据 LLM 是被什么训练出来的来改我们的教育？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, hopefully we don't change it just so that we ask, we get students who are like, "Hey, here's a thousand words. Predict the next one."
turns.zh: 是啊，希望我们不会把它改成那样：学生们说「嘿，这里给你一千个词，预测下一个」。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Just read it all.
turns.zh: 全读完就行了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Keep it all in your head.
turns.zh: 全记在脑子里。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah. Let me come back to this safety piece because I think there's a lot of people that are just worried about where things are going. And I'm curious just as someone watching this stuff happen, being within the alignment org, watching it evolve, are you optimistic we'll figure it out?
turns.zh: 对。说回安全这块，因为很多人都对未来感到担忧。我很好奇，作为一个亲眼看着这一切发生、又身处对齐组织内部看着它演化的人，你乐观吗？你觉得我们能解决它吗？

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Do you think we'll crack this and keep AI aligned with our interests?
turns.zh: 你觉得我们会攻克这个问题，让 AI 始终和我们的利益保持一致吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: My take on this is I'm personally optimistic. I think this is something where right now a lot of people are paying attention to it. And first of all, I think that's kind of a great thing. I think as an issue like this rises in prominence, it's exactly what we were talking about earlier. It's like this technology is powerful, it has benefits, it has risks.
turns.zh: 我的看法是，我个人是乐观的。我觉得眼下很多人都在关注这件事，这本身就是件好事。首先我觉得这很棒。你看，当这样的议题越来越受关注时，这恰好就是我们前面聊过的：这项技术很强大，它有好处，也有风险。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We have to adapt and shift resources from benefits to risks and back and forth as it progresses. And so to me, I feel like we've continued to study it.
turns.zh: 随着它发展，我们得不断调整，把资源在好处和风险之间来回挪。所以对我来说，我感觉我们一直在研究它。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The thing that's interesting is that as the models get better, they get in some ways easier to study. And so there's been this sort of strange... The models get better and so the world model inside them is clearer and we can understand some parts of them better, but also to get more capable.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，随着模型变强，它们在某些方面反而变得更容易研究。于是出现了一种奇怪的情况：模型变强了，它们内部的世界模型更清晰，我们能更好地理解它们的一部分，但同时它们也变得更强大。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so they're more able to evade basic measures of security. And so there's this push and pull as models get better. And I think basically based on this push and pull, you want to allocate more or less resources to various parts of monitoring, understanding their circuits better, things like that.
turns.zh: 而更强也意味着它们更有能力规避基本的防护手段。所以模型变强的过程中始终有这股推拉。我觉得基本上就是根据这股推拉，来决定往监控、更好地理解它们的回路等等方向上分配多少资源。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: But it's also why I'm happy to chat with you because one of the main things that I think is important to make progress is just to make sure that people understand both what kind of systems these are, how they work, how they're made, so they can form good mental models of the present, of the future, and so they can decide how to shape it, whether that's taking part in some of these alignment efforts or just informing them as the public that's going to have to vote and decide on much of these issues. I don't know. I'm pretty excited for this current moment we're in for that reason.
turns.zh: 但这也是为什么我很乐意来跟你聊：我觉得要取得进展，最重要的一件事之一，就是确保人们理解这些究竟是什么样的系统、它们怎么运作、又是怎么造出来的，这样他们才能对当下、对未来形成好的心智模型，从而决定要怎么塑造它——不管是参与这些对齐工作，还是作为将来必须在诸多问题上投票和做决定的公众，去充分知情。我不知道。就这一点而言，我对当下这个时刻相当期待。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And something I think people misunderstand is people working in these labs have taken this problem very seriously from the beginning. Like I said, Anthropic's original mission was AI safety and alignment. That was the reason that it became a company.
turns.zh: 还有一点我觉得人们误解了：在这些实验室工作的人，从一开始就非常认真地对待这个问题。就像我说的，Anthropic 最初的使命就是 AI 安全与对齐，这是它之所以成为一家公司的原因。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And a lot of people are hearing this for the first time or think that it's not a serious area of study and that people aren't focused on it, but many smart people care a lot about this and are working on it. And there's a lot of... From what I can tell, a lot of good progress is happening.
turns.zh: 很多人是第一次听到这些，或者觉得这不是一个正经的研究方向、大家并不上心；但其实有很多聪明人非常在意这件事，并在为之工作。而且据我所知，这里面正在发生很多很好的进展。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The other point you made about the models growing very smoothly in intelligence, there's been this question of are we going to have a fast takeoff or a slow takeoff? There's always this fear that we would hit a point or curse of self-improvement, for example, and just takes off super intelligence, we're huge trouble, we have no control, it's out of the box.
turns.zh: 你刚才还提到模型智力在非常平滑地增长，这就引出了另一个问题：我们会迎来快速起飞还是缓慢起飞？人们一直害怕某种「自我改进的诅咒」——比如某个临界点一过，超级智能突然起飞，我们麻烦大了，完全失去控制，它已经出盒了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: But it feels very much like we're on the slow takeoff scenario because as you said, the models are kind of very smoothly improving and where we are catching the little things along the way, learning, evolving, putting regulation around it. So of the scenarios, this feels like a pretty good path we're on of the many scenarios people imagined and the fears they had.
turns.zh: 但感觉很像是我们正处在缓慢起飞这个情景里：正如你所说，模型在非常平滑地改进，而我们在沿途捕捉那些小问题、学习、演化、并且在周围建立监管。所以在人们想象过的众多情景和恐惧里，这一条看起来是我们走在一条相当不错的路上。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: As this pace of progress evolves, it's just a matter of reacting quickly.
turns.zh: 随着这种进步速度继续演进，说到底就是快速反应的问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: That's why I think having people be informed is great because then people will voice concerns or voice their opinions and then regularly evaluating what the benefits are, what the risks are and how we mitigate each is basically the way that feels like the right way forward.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得让人们知情是件好事，因为这样人们会表达关切、表达意见，然后定期重新评估好处是什么、风险是什么、以及各自怎么缓解——这基本就是我认为正确的推进方式。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And yeah, I kind of agree with you that it feels like there's momentum to do this right now, which is great.
turns.zh: 对，我也多少同意你的看法：现在这股把事情做好的势头是存在的，这很好。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Something I wanted to ask you, completely unrelated, where are you on the simulation hypothesis? Being someone that watches all this life form growing, are you more convinced we're in a simulation and we're not at the base layer of all this, or not?
turns.zh: 有件我特别想问的事，跟前面完全无关：你在「模拟假说」上是什么立场？作为一个看着这种生命形式不断生长的人，你是否更相信我们身处一个模拟之中、并不是这一切的最底层？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, this is a fun one. I actually haven't thought about this in a while. To me, there's something else that looking inside these models brings out, which is this sort of almost like there's a fundamental structure that they keep falling on.
turns.zh: 哦，这个话题挺有意思。我其实有一阵子没想过这个了。对我来说，往这些模型内部看还带出了另一样东西：几乎可以说，它们总是落在某种根本性的结构上。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: This is really to your question, I promise. Let me get to it. Let me explain. I've studied a bunch of Claude models and also some different models, some open source work. And then a lot of time when you look at what they learn and what the structure inside is, it's surprisingly similar.
turns.zh: 这真的是在回答你的问题，我保证。我解释一下。我研究过不少 Claude 模型，也看过一些别的模型、一些开源的工作。很多时候你去看它们学到了什么、内部的构造是什么，会发现相似得惊人。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And this is for models that are trained years apart on different data by different people and you look at how they solve these problems and there's just so much overlap. And my take on why that is that for some problems that are important, there's just one efficient way to do things.
turns.zh: 而且这是些训练年份相隔、数据不同、由不同团队训练出来的模型，你去看它们怎么解决这些问题，重叠之处非常多。我的看法是：对于一些重要的问题，只有一条高效的解法。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's kind of one way to do math efficiently that fits the structure of our brain and we all learn it and very few people are doing it a crazy different way. Everybody works in base 10, not many people in base six or whatever.
turns.zh: 比如数学只有一种高效的算法恰好契合我们大脑的结构，我们全都学会了它，很少有人用一种完全不一样的方式去做。大家都用十进制，很少有人用六进制之类的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think that to me makes me think that there's some fundamental structure of information that these models are picking up on, that in some ways we're picking up on, and maybe a crazier simulation level that kind of is like regularity in our world.
turns.zh: 这对我来说让我觉得：存在某种信息的根本结构，这些模型捕捉到了，我们在某种意义上也捕捉到了；而在更疯狂一点的层面上，也许那就是我们世界里的某种规律性。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so that maybe makes me think that if you were to have the power to simulate something like our world, actually you would land in a similar situation. There's just kind of this basin of where things end up and they're just the easiest way for things to arrange themselves. And so in that sense, maybe. Yeah.
turns.zh: 所以这可能让我觉得：如果你有能力去模拟一个像我们这样的世界，你实际上也会落到一个类似的位置上。事情就是有一个「汇流处」，那是它们最容易自我安排的方式。所以从这个意义上说，也许吧。对，我可以相信我们身处模拟之中。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I could believe that we're in a simulation. I think I'm not sure I fully buy it. The other reason I don't fully buy it is that even though I think the structure lends itself to it, there'd be a question of why? Who's running this, and for what? And that one, I don't know about.
turns.zh: 不过我不太完全买账。另一个我不完全接受的理由是：即便我认为这个结构让它说得通，还是会留下一个问题——为什么？谁在运行这一切？为了什么？这一点我不知道。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Well, something Elon said has stuck with me about this, that if you were to run a simulation, it'd be an interesting time in history or something that you're really excited about, and it tracks that this is a very interesting time in history.
turns.zh: 有句 Elon 说的话我一直记着：如果是你在运行一个模拟，那会是一个有意思的历史时刻，或者说你会对此非常兴奋；而这也确实对应上——这是一个非常有意思的历史时刻。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yes. Yeah. Okay. That's a fair point. That's a fair point.
turns.zh: 对，对。好吧，这话说得在理，这话说得在理。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Data centers and space and robots and artificial intelligence.
turns.zh: 数据中心、太空、机器人，还有人工智能。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. Okay. I see it now. I see it now. Yeah. Somebody recently told me they used to think that may you live in interesting times was a blessing and they're not so sure now. They're like, "The boring times are pretty good too."
turns.zh: 对。好，我明白了，我明白了。对。最近有人跟我说，他们以前觉得「愿你生活在有趣的时代」是一种祝福，现在不太确定了。他们说：「无聊的时代也挺不错的。」

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Oh, man. And then there's an Emmanuel out there watching your thinking process in your JSpace.
turns.zh: 天哪。而且还有个 Emmanuel 在外面，通过你的 JSpace 盯着你的思考过程。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh my God. Yeah. Hopefully I'm making him proud. He's not like, "Oh, I got to rerun the simulation. We messed up this one."
turns.zh: 我的天。是啊。希望我让他感到骄傲。他不会说：「哦，我得重跑一遍模拟。这一次我们搞砸了。」

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Shut it down. No. Oh, man. Okay. One last question randomly out of nowhere. So Swyx, who runs AI engineering, latent space podcast, awesome guy, I asked him what to ask you. You were on his podcast a year ago and something completely from a different direction.
turns.zh: 关掉它。不。天哪。好。最后一个完全不相干的问题。Swyx——他做 AI engineering、办 Latent Space 播客，超厉害——我问他该问你什么。他说你一年前上过他的播客，他想问一个完全不同方向的东西。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: He wanted to get your take on Jev, which is this hot new model that recently came out that is very fast making decisions. OpenAI, funny enough, just launched their own version a week later. Thoughts on Jev in the space of quick decision-based models?
turns.zh: 他想知道你怎么看 Jev——最近出来的热门新模型，决策非常快。有意思的是，OpenAI 恰好在一周后也发布了他们自己的版本。你怎么看 Jev，以及这类快速决策模型？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, right. So my take on Jev is these kind of models, you give them some context and you give them a few options to choose between and they just are very quick at choosing an option for you. To me, it's impossible not to hear about this and think of system one thinking versus system two or something.
turns.zh: 好，说到 Jev，我的看法是：这类模型，你给它一些上下文，再给它几个选项让它选，它就会非常快地帮你选出一个。对我来说，听到这个不可能不想起「系统一思维」和「系统二思维」之类的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: A lot of what I've studied with these models is how they sample one token with the Claude models. And so you can think of these decision models as pretty similar. Take an LLM and sample one token. They're different important ways, but at a fundamental level, you can be like, oh, you're not letting the model sample and reason. It's just your gut feeling.
turns.zh: 我研究这些模型时做的很大一部分工作，是研究 Claude 模型如何采样出一个 token。所以你可以把这类决策模型看作相当类似：拿一个 LLM，只采样一个 token。它们有一些重要的区别，但在根本层面上，你可以说：哦，你没有让模型去采样和推理，这只是你的直觉。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Is the answer A or is the answer B? To me, that seems like something that's...
turns.zh: 答案是 A 还是 B？在我看来，这似乎是某种……

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: That general frame of sometimes you'll just want a binary decision or one out of 10 or whatever is just clearly, I don't know, both clearly useful and something that I imagine is probably going to be a part of intelligent systems where for some stuff, you need to think about a long time.
turns.zh: 这种大框架——有时候你就是要一个二选一的决定，或者十选一之类的——显然、我是说，两头都显然有用；而且我猜它很可能会成为智能系统里的一个组成部分：有些事你需要想很久。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's like what's our roadmap for the next year? You need to think about it for a while. And then for some stuff where it's like, is this person who wrote us a review happy or upset? You're happy with the gut judgment. So yeah, I think this kind of research is cool and I think it's also different from the...
turns.zh: 比如「我们明年的路线图是什么？」这个你得想上一阵子。而有些事，比如「这个给我们写评价的人是高兴还是不高兴？」用直觉判断就够了。所以对，我觉得这类研究很有意思，而且它跟我们见过的那些 LLM 有点不一样。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's a bit of a novel take on some of the LLMs we've seen. So yeah, I'm pretty excited to see where this kind of stuff goes.
turns.zh: 它是对我们见过的某些 LLM 的一种有点新奇的切入。所以对，我很期待看到这类东西会走向哪里。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So I'm hearing here is this going to be a new foundational component most likely of AI and LLMs. And the system one, system two stuff is basically Kahneman's... I have that book up there actually behind me. System one, just to keep it simple, is just your amygdala limbic system making just gut-level quick decisions like, "Snake, oh no-"
turns.zh: 所以我的理解是：这很可能会成为 AI 和 LLM 的一个新的基础组件。而系统一、系统二这套东西基本上就是卡尼曼的……其实那本书就在我身后放着。简单说，系统一就是你的边缘系统（limbic system）做出的那种凭直觉的快速决定，比如「蛇！糟了——」

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where you don't have to think long about it. It's to protect you from bad things really easily and quickly. And system two is where we really think about stuff and process.
turns.zh: 你不需要长时间思考的，它是为了让你又准又快地躲开坏事。而系统二才是我们真正思考和处理事情的地方。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，完全正确。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Sweet. Emmanuel, is there anything else that we haven't covered? Anything else you want to say or mention? Anything you want to double down on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 好。Emmanuel，还有什么我们没聊到的吗？还有什么你想说、想提的？在我们进入非常精彩的快问快答环节之前，还有什么想再强调一下的吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I'm definitely curious for folks' takes always on some of the stuff that is still unexplored or didn't make sense. There's a lot more interp experiments than we have the time to share. Models have a bunch of weird little things about them. Maybe I'll do a lightning round of weird little things if that's okay.
turns.zh: 我一直很想听听大家对那些还没被探索清楚、或者没被理解的东西的看法。我们能分享的可解释性实验远比你以为的多。模型身上有各种各样古怪的小细节。如果可以的话，我干脆来一轮「古怪的小事」快问快答？

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Let's do it. Absolutely.
turns.zh: 来吧，当然可以。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Okay. Weird little thing one, we found that models can actually answer questions obviously. They can do math or you can ask them what's the color of a banana?
turns.zh: 好。古怪的小事第一件：我们发现模型当然能回答问题。它们会做数学，或者你问它们「香蕉是什么颜色」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And if you look inside, you'll see all these intermediate steps, but they have a separate mechanism which is a gut check and which is totally different and which is just as they reason, they'll have some part of them that will flag something's wrong.
turns.zh: 而如果你往里看，会看到所有这些中间步骤，但它们还有一个独立的机制，叫做「直觉校验」，跟前面完全不同：就在它们推理的过程中，会有一部分把它们标记出来——「有东西不对」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: If a model somehow says four plus five equals 23 or something, and there's a part of the model that just reads that and doesn't do the math, but it's just like that can't be right because four plus five, definitely under 10. And so they learn these weird hunches, they feel like a hunch.
turns.zh: 比如模型不知怎么说出「四加五等于 23」，而模型里有一部分会读到这个，它根本没去做这个加法，只是说：这不可能，因为四加五肯定小于 10。所以它们会学到这些古怪的直觉，像一种「感觉」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Maybe another one is you can tell the model, "Hey, do this task and think about this other thing," and then you can use interp to see if there's intermediate representations that map to the other thing, and that works. You see that it does think about the other thing.
turns.zh: 另一件可能是：你可以对模型说「嘿，做这个任务的时候也想想另一件事」，然后用可解释性去看有没有对应的中间表示，而这个是成立的。你能看到它确实想了那件事。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: This is something that's really mysterious to me because there's no kind of training reason why the model would have to learn that. So it's another one of these weird behaviors. Actually, maybe I'll keep it at two. I think those two are good enough.
turns.zh: 这件事对我来说非常神秘，因为训练上没有任何理由要求模型必须学会这个。所以它又是另一件古怪的行为。其实我可能就讲两个吧，我觉得这两个就够了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Just what a fun job. This is just studying this thing and trying to understand what the hell is going on. How is it getting this smart? How does it think? How many people are even in this space? Just how large is this field?
turns.zh: 这工作听起来真有意思。就是研究这个东西，试着搞明白到底怎么回事。它怎么变得这么聪明的？它是怎么思考的？这个领域里到底有多少人在做？这个领域有多大？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The field itself is getting pretty large. I would say maybe hundreds, not thousands. There's different interp people at the different labs and then there's, in academia, quite a few labs putting out great work.
turns.zh: 这个领域本身已经相当大了。我会说，几百人吧，不是几千人。各个实验室都有做可解释性的人，学界也有好几个实验室在做很棒的工作。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: If someone were to get into this space, is it like an ML person usually or is there a neuroscientist track to get into this?
turns.zh: 如果有人想进入这个领域，通常是机器学习背景的人吗？还是说也有一条神经科学家的路径可以走？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, there's actually a surprising amount of ex-neuroscientists. I do think in order to get in the field, it doesn't require a lot of prior knowledge because it's such a new field.
turns.zh: 实际上，转行过来的神经科学家数量惊人。但我确实觉得进入这个领域不需要太多前置知识，因为它是个非常新的领域。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So the on-ramp is mostly, I would say, self-studying and reading some of the key papers. And then there's actually... Yeah, maybe I should give a plug. There's actually websites like neuronpedia.org I think is the URL, which are open source interp. They host a bunch of models and let you do interp experiments on them.
turns.zh: 所以上手的路径主要是自学加读几篇关键论文。而且其实……对，我可能该给个推荐。像 neuronpedia.org——我记得网址是这个——这类网站做的是开源的可解释性：它们托管了一批模型，让你自己在上面做可解释性实验。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So many people have just been doing that on their own. I think that there's so much to explore that if you're at all curious, you should just give it a try.
turns.zh: 很多人就是自己这么干起来的。我觉得有那么多东西可以探索，只要你稍微有点好奇，就该动手试试。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That's awesome. We'll link to that in the show notes in case that's not the right URL.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会在节目笔记里放上链接，以防我记错网址。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Cool.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Well, Emmanuel, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好，那 Emmanuel，说到这里，我们就进入非常精彩的快问快答环节了。我准备了五个问题。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I am as ready as I'll ever be.
turns.zh: 我从来就没有这么准备好过。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Here we go. What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: One I read recently is A Brief History of Intelligence. It's this really cool book that walks through the history of basically brains and five key moments in our evolution that sort of bootstrapped these brain systems on top of one another. It's super accessible.
turns.zh: 我最近读的一本是《A Brief History of Intelligence》（《智能简史》）。这本书特别棒，它梳理了大脑的历史，讲我们进化中的五个关键时刻，是怎么一层层把大脑系统「搭」起来的。非常好读，一点也不需要神经科学的背景。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: You don't need any neuroscience knowledge or anything. Another one is Stories of Your Life and Others. This is Ted Chiang. This is maybe my favorite sci-fi book of all time. It's a bunch of short stories.
turns.zh: 你完全不需要任何神经科学知识。另一本是《Stories of Your Life and Others》（《你一生的故事及其他》），Ted Chiang 写的。这可能是我这辈子最喜欢的科幻书。里面是一组短篇小说。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It does what I think is the high art version of sci-fi where it's just take one weird idea, like what if this happened, and then write a story of just what would the world look like if that happened? It's truly excellent.
turns.zh: 它做的是我觉得科幻的最高艺术形态：取一个古怪的假设，比如「如果这件事发生了会怎样」，然后写一个故事，讲真发生了的话世界会是什么样子。真的非常出色。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I think I have that in my bookshelf behind me too. Also highly recommend that one. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 我觉得我身后书架上也有那本。同样强烈推荐。最近最喜欢的电影或者剧集是什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Okay. One popular one, one deep cut. Obsession was my favorite movie of the year. It's a horror movie, so don't go if you hate horror movies.
turns.zh: 好，一个大众的，一个冷门的。《Obsession》是我今年最喜欢的电影。它是恐怖片，所以如果你讨厌恐怖片就别去。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: No, thank you.
turns.zh: 不了，谢谢。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, no. Even if you're open to a horror movie, you should go because it was just so fresh. You know how movies, I feel like if you've seen a lot, sometimes you're like, "Oh, it's another... I've seen this many times. This one was just so new, so fresh." And I'll say one thing about it, which is that it takes a lot of rom-com tropes and subverts them to be spooky.
turns.zh: 哎，不。即使你对恐怖片持开放态度，也该去看看，因为它实在太新鲜了。你知道电影这事，我觉得你看过很多之后，有时会想「哦，又是这个……这种我都看过了」。而这一部就是那么新、那么新鲜。我要说它一点：它把大量爱情喜剧的老套路颠覆过来变成恐怖元素。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think that that's just a brilliant, brilliant way to make a movie. And then I'm French, so there's a TV show that came out this year called Bref Du. Bref is French for brief.
turns.zh: 我觉得那真是极妙的拍电影方式。然后我是法国人，所以今年有部剧叫《Bref Du》。《Bref》在法语里是「简报」的意思。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Brief used to be this cult classic in France 15 years ago, and they came up with a sequel many years into the making and you can watch it. I had a bunch of American friends that have watched it. It's got subtitles and it's just this incredibly... Again, it's novel. The editing is crazy.
turns.zh: 它有字幕，而且它极其……对，它非常新鲜。剪辑疯了一般。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: They are just extremely creative and it's very short, so I would recommend that.
turns.zh: 他们极有创造力，而且很短，所以我推荐这个。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Favorite product you recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 最近发现并且很喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I love my Apple Watch and I hate that it charges or I have to charge it every day. I bought the Apple Watch Ultra just recently, and man, that is so nice. If you've ever been frustrated by this good product that somehow we can't figure out how to give a good battery to, well, it turns out if you make it bigger, the battery's better. So I've been happy with that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢我的 Apple Watch，也讨厌它要充电、我得每天充一次。我最近买了 Apple Watch Ultra，天哪，那太爽了。如果你也曾被这种「明明是好产品、但厂商就是没法给它做出好续航」的事烦到过——结果就是，把它做大，续航就变好了。所以我用得很开心。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to often in work or in life?
turns.zh: 你有没有一句人生格言，在工作或者生活里会反复回到它？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's one nonfiction book that really is probably my favorite ever. It's 4,000 Weeks. It has a lot in it that I think is cool. One of the cool things is this sort of thing that was really relevant to me, which is that the when I finally mentality is a common mentality and it's kind of toxic. So what does that mean?
turns.zh: 有一本非虚构的书，可能是我这辈子最喜欢的一本：《4,000 Weeks》（《四千周》）。里面有很多我觉得很棒的东西。其中一个特别打动我的点是所谓「等我终于……的心态」——这种心态很常见，而且有点有毒。这是什么意思呢？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's sort of this, when I finally check off all the items on my to-do list, I'll finally be able to chill. When I finally get married, I'll be happy. When I finally get a promotion. And this is sort of, I mean, you were talking about meditation.
turns.zh: 大概是这样：等我把待办清单上的事全都划掉，我终于可以放松了。等我终于结婚了，我就会快乐。等我终于升职了……而这跟你刚才说的冥想有点关系。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: This is almost the opposite of meditation and that at the end of the day, your life is all of the moments you lived in the moment and that there's this sense in which you should just try to always be in the moment and not projecting yourself towards a future that seems better. Probably if you're telling yourself, "When I finally do X, I'll be happy," when you do X, you will not be happy.
turns.zh: 这几乎是冥想的反面：说到底，你的人生就是你当时活过的那些瞬间；所以你其实应该尽量始终活在当下，而不是把自己投射到一个看起来更好的未来上。如果你在告诉自己「等我终于做完 X，我就会快乐」，那等你真做完 X，你是不会快乐的。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Is there a better phrase to use or is it just don't do that? Do they say-
turns.zh: 有没有更好的说法？还是说就是「别这样」？书里有没有讲——

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I don't know. I think to me the positive version is be in the moment. I appreciate the moment. There was a blog post recently I read that was... I forget. It was something like enjoy the sandwich, I think it was literally the sentence. I don't know if you saw this where somebody was like, "Yeah, you're eating a sandwich, you've eaten many sandwiches. Enjoy the sandwich.
turns.zh: 我不确定。对我来说，积极一点的说法是：活在当下，珍惜当下。我最近读过一篇博客，是……我忘了，大概是「享受这个三明治」这句话，字面意思就是这句。我不知道你有没有看过，有人说：「对，你在吃三明治，你已经吃过很多三明治了。享受这个三明治。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: You're in a team meeting. Yeah, you've been in many..." Be in it and not looking towards the next thing.
turns.zh: 你在开团队会议，你已经开过很多次了……」活在当下，而不是一直望向下一件事。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I did a meditation retreat once. It was a 10-day silent retreat where you eat silently too and no one's talking. You just sit there and eat your food. And I just remember peeling an egg for five minutes and just noticing every shell piece and just the smell of it all. And it's hard to get into that mode, but it's such an interesting place to be where everything is just interesting. Come on, look at this egg versus just stuff through my mouth.
turns.zh: 我参加过一次冥想静修（retreat），是十天的静默场，连吃饭都得沉默，也没人说话。你就坐在那儿吃东西。我记得我剥一个鸡蛋剥了五分钟，就注意每一块蛋壳、还有它的气味。那种状态很难进入，但那是个特别有意思的位置——在那里，一切都是有意思的。来，看这个鸡蛋，而不是直接把它塞进嘴里。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, right. While you're on Slack with your left hand and listening to a podcast at the same time.
turns.zh: 对，就在你左手还挂着 Slack、同时还在听播客的时候。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Oh, man. Okay. Final question. You study AI all day. You watching AI, how things... If an AI were to look inside your brain, what would be surprising? What would it see that might surprise people?
turns.zh: 天哪。好。最后一个问题：你一整天都在研究 AI，看着 AI，看着那些事情……如果一个 AI 往你脑子里看，它会发现什么令人惊讶的事？它会看到什么可能让人吃惊的东西？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Surely my deepest, darkest secrets, but what are the-
turns.zh: 肯定是我那些最深最黑的秘密，不过——

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Let's get into it. Let's get into it.
turns.zh: 说来听听，说来听听。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, man. I've always been a bit of a jokester or that's just both how I live and how I cope. I just think that even in serious situations, you should aim to have some levity.
turns.zh: 哎，我一直有点像个段子手，或者说这既是我活着的方式，也是我的应对方式。我就是觉得，即便在严肃的场合，你也应该努力保留一点轻松。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so I think if you looked inside my brain, you'd definitely be surprised that basically at any given moment I'm just focusing on some random thing that is funny. I'll be in a serious meeting and I'll be like, "Oh yeah, but isn't it kind of random that you're wearing this random thing?" Or something.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得如果你往我脑子里看，你肯定会惊讶地发现：基本上任何时刻，我脑子里都在想某个随机的好笑的事。我会在一个严肃的会议里想：「哦对了，你戴这个随机的东西，不是挺有意思的吗？」之类的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's just like I have these intrusive thoughts that I keep out, but that are all usually just bad jokes. And sometimes as you've heard today, unfortunately they come out, so I'm sorry for those, but that's probably the most surprising thing.
turns.zh: 我脑子里有一些侵入性的念头，我一般压着不说，但通常都是些烂梗。有时候——如你今天听到的——不幸它们会冒出来，所以这些我道歉，不过那大概是最令人惊讶的部分了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I love that. Emmanuel, thank you so much for being here. Final question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。Emmanuel，非常感谢你来做客。最后一个问题：听众可以怎样帮到你？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Just do some interp, read about how the models work. I mean, you mentioned Dwarkesh writeup. I think it was great as well. I think this is such a new field, both interp and AI and LLMs, and I think it just benefits from people engaging and being informed. So read things.
turns.zh: 做点可解释性，读读这些模型是怎么运作的东西。我是说，你提到了 Dwarkesh 的那篇文章，我觉得写得也很好。这是个非常新的领域，无论是可解释性还是 AI、LLM 都是。我觉得它就是从更多人的参与和知情中受益。所以，多读。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: If there's more that you would want to know about how these models work that we haven't figured out, you can reach out to me. I'm on a variety of social platforms, probably you can reach out to me on X.
turns.zh: 如果你还想知道更多关于这些模型怎么运作、而我们还没搞清楚的事，你可以联系我。我在好几个社交平台上都有，大概你可以在 X 上找到我。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: We'll link to some of the videos that you guys have put out that describe a lot of the stuff we've been talking about, like JSpace and things like that. There's some really beautiful videos your team has made. I don't know who does that, but they're really cool.
turns.zh: 我们会放上你们团队做的几个视频的链接，里面讲了我们刚才聊的很多东西，比如 JSpace 之类的。你们团队做的有些视频非常漂亮，我不知道是谁做的，但真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. We partner with our design team, so all credit goes to them for the cool videos.
turns.zh: 对。我们跟设计团队合作，所以那些酷酷的视频得归功于他们。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Amazing. All right. Well, thank you again, Emmanuel. Thank you so much for doing this. This was amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，再次谢谢你，Emmanuel，非常感谢你来做这期节目，太棒了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Thanks, Lenny. Yeah, this was super fun.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Lenny。对，这期超级有意思。
